subsubtopic: PROPOSED FREE TRADE-CALL FOR GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and privilege to present a petition that has been certified correct according to Standing Order 106. Yet again, my petition is on the subject of the Government's trade arrangement with the United States.
The people who have signed this petition believe that it will have a fundamental impact on Canada's economic, cultural and political independence. They also believe the agreement implies the loss of jobs in many sectors and regions of this country.
Therefore they request that the Parliament of Canada obtain a clear mandate from the people of Canada through a national debate on the alternatives available to this country and that this debate result in a national election prior to the implementation of any such agreement.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise and present the first address on Bill C-105, the Railway Safety Act. I would like to express my appreciation to the Government House Leader for making earnest efforts to have this Bill called yesterday, but given the fluid nature of this House, that was impossible. I would much rather be in the Crow's Nest Pass handing our Olympic coins to people in the Crow's Nest, Cowley, Pincher Creek, Fort MacLeod and Brocket, but that was impossible. However, I will complete the rest of the circuit in my riding this evening.
The Railway Safety Act is part of the total transport modernization of air, marine and railways. This Parliament has already passed Bill C-18, the National Transportation Act. It has passed Bill C-19, the Motor Vehicle Transport Act. It has passed Bill C-21, the Shipping Conferences Act. It has passed Bill C-75 dealing with the Canada Shipping Act, and Bill C-52 respecting the coasting trade is at a legislative
Railway Safety Act
committee right at this moment. Bill C-105, after two or three days, will go to the standing committee, and there is yet to come legislation respecting the transportation accident investigation board. Therefore, you can see, Mr. Speaker, that this Parliament has been active in the field of transportation. I believe this Parliament has acted wisely in those Bills because it is an area in which there has not been much legislative activity for quite some time.
In broad terms, the new transportation agency will look after economic regulation of all modes of transport in this country. The Ministry of Transport will be responsible for safety regulation. The next Bill, establishing the Transportation Accident Investigation Board, for the information of Members, will set up a quasi-judicial, totally independent accident investigation board, similar to the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, but will cover air, railway and marine. In terms of broad principles, I think it is a wise principle to have a separation of those three interests.
In general terms, this railway safety legislation includes all the legislative recommendations of Mr. Justice Foisy after the tragic Hinton accident. It brings safety into the Ministry of Transport. It streamlines many of the processes in the Bill, as I will set forth. It stresses inspection of operating and maintenance rather than what is contained in the existing legislation with its emphasis on construction. It sets up a consultative railway safety committee. It imposes the existing criminal law that applies to everyone in cars, trucks, airplanes and boats to people operating trains. It has a five year review, which I think Hon. Members who are knowledgeable in the area know is in the statute, although other Members might not be aware of it.
The next major point is that in spite of the fact that we have had some tragic accidents-and even one accident is too many-in relative terms Canada is a safe place. The railways are responsible for only some 3 per cent of transportation accidents. CP has been the safest railway in all of North America in seven of the last eleven years. CN is consistently within the top six.
It is fair to say that the introduction of this Bill is confirmation of the Government's political commitment to ensure that safety has first priority in the Canadian transportation system. As Members know, amendments to the Aeronautics Act were passed in 1985 which addressed the safety of Canadian aviation. This was followed up with action to strengthen security at Canadian airports.
In 1987 the House passed amendments to the Canada Shipping Act which dealt primarily with safety. Further steps have been taken to improve navigational safety through measures for vessel traffic control and new safety requirements for offshore drilling rigs.
Of greatest interest to all Canadians is road safety. We have taken the lead in promoting the use of seatbelts. Of course, we have established a requirement for daytime running lights on

February 4, 1988
Railway Safety Act
new vehicles sold in this country, starting later this year. Our commitment to safety in transportation was established as a central tenet of government policy in Section 3 of the National Transportation Act, 1987, Bill C-18. This statement clearly set forth safety as the first objective of transportation legislation by requiring that "the transportation system meet the highest practicable safety standards".
The Bill now before the House has been prepared to implement this policy for the railways of Canada. The Railway Safety Act will be followed in the near future by a Bill to create a transportation accident investigation board. This independent board will be empowered to investigate all accidents in all federally-regulated modes of transportation, drawing upon expert staff to determine causes and to recommend means to prevent any recurrence.
By way of background, Hon. Members will know that for many years the safety of Canada's railways has been regulated under the Railway Act. This Act originated at the turn of the century, at a time when the railway system was rapidly expanding. This growth brought with it an increasing need for safety regulation.
At that time much of Canada's railway system was under construction to open up new territory and to encourage settlement. Lines were often speculative, built into new territory where revenue potential was very low. Some smaller companies lacked cash and were tempted to cut corners on construction and operation. Trains were short, slow, few and far between. Then, and for many years, trains were controlled by instructions sent by telegraph to wayside stations with handwritten messages "hooped-up" to the crew of a passing train on the end of a bamboo stick.
The environment has changed. Canada's railways are moving huge volumes of freight, be it containers from Montreal to southern Ontario, automobiles from Toronto to the Prairies, or bulk commodities: grain, sulphur, potash and coal from the West to the export terminals. Along the way the trains themselves have grown enormously-15,000 tonne trains are now commonplace compared to the 200 tonne or 300 tonne trains that were the norm when the Railway Act was first conceived.
Today's large trains move faster and over longer distances without stopping than ever before. More and more dangerous commodities have been added, often moving through busy urban corridors. Large scale movement of dangerous goods was unheard of when the Railway Act was first written. I notice in the House again today the presence of the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) who has spoken so often in Question Period and who is vitally concerned about the railway safety in the Toronto metropolitan areas.
Today, railways are in the midst of a technological revolution. Sophisticated communications equipment and computer systems are being developed to control the movement of trains. A major new development will soon transmit train movement
instructions directly by radio to computers on board locomotives.
Recently, the Minister announced that the Government is providing funding to encourage this development known as the advanced train control system. The railways are making large investments in high technology with much more to come. It is a matter of survival, for the industry is under strong competitive pressure.
The changing environment was reflected in the report of the Commission of Inquiry into the Hinton Train Collision. Justice Foisy stated his concern that Government is not keeping apace with the need to modernize rules and regulations. The railways have simply changed but not the legislation. It is becoming more and more difficult for the railway safety regulator to respond to the changing environment while working under the existing Railway Act.
As I said earlier, the Railway Act was created to cover all aspects of railway regulation. It combines in a confusing melange safety regulation, economic regulation and accident investigation, along with an assortment of sections governing telegraph systems and railway corporate affairs. The combination of safety and economic regulations and accident investigation in one agency of Government is now recognized not to be in the public interest. There is a potential for conflict among these responsibilities. While I hasten to add that no such conflict was evident in the performance of the Canadian Transport Commission it is a possibility, and thus the policy of the Government, to separate these responsibilities.
The existing legislation is riddled with anachronisms. For instance, the Railway Act legislates the weight of bells for steam locomotives. The railway of the last century was in many respects a dangerous workplace. Legislative protection for employees was created in areas that would cause surprise today, such as in a specific Railway Act provision prohibiting the oiling of steam locomotive valves while the engine is moving. This questionable practice, not to mention the steam locomotive itself, disappeared many years ago.
Railway construction a century ago was often a hit and miss affair with public and employee safety sometimes taking second place. What the industry could not or would not do, the Government of the day had to undertake. The result was a legislated requirement for the regulator to become directly involved in the details of railway construction. This placed a burden of evaluation and approval of routine construction projects on the Government. Now, with universally-accepted standards of engineering, more protective labour legislation and a stable and mature railway industry, many of these regulatory activities are unproductive.
A review of railway accidents over the past 10 years to 20 years or more shows that the construction of railway track and structures is not the source of safety problems on the railways today. Resources, which now must be committed to approval and inspection of construction projects, could be used to far greater safety effect elsewhere. Performance of these duties by
February 4, 1988

the regulator can even be interpreted as removing some of the responsibility for compliance with safety standards from railway management, which is where it really belongs.
The existing legislation imposes on railway rule making the review of publication procedures for government regulations. These procedures were designed to protect the rights and privacy of individuals. They were not intended to deal with technical aspects of railway operations. The Government regulator and the industry face serious delays when making needed changes to operating rules, simply because the Railway Act requires it. Mr. Justice Foisy was sufficiently concerned about these delays to specifically recommend that the Government "take immediate steps to make the uniform code of operating rules current, and to maintain it in that condition". It is difficult, if not impossible, to do so under the provisions of the existing Railway Act.
[DOT] (M30)
Today our safety concerns focus on how the railways operate and maintain heavy density main lines involving the movement of 15,000 tonne freight trains, and passenger trains carrying hundreds of people. Yet the Railway Act only created powers of inspection for engineers.
The penalties found in the Railway Act make interesting reading. An engineer can be fined $8 for failing to blow his whistle at a crossing, while a multimillion dollar corporation may face a fine of SI00. The Railway Act also contains the somewhat quaint threat of punishment by hard labour.
The message is obvious. Railway transportation and the transportation environment have changed in the past, and are changing rapidly today. The legislation must meet the challenge.
When the Minister tabled the railway safety Bill, he also released a report on drug and alcohol abuse in the railway industry. The Minister has asked for comments from the public on recommendations in that report dealing with mandatory drug testing before proposing any government action to Cabinet. Nevertheless, he indicated that this was an issue that should also be discussed by members of the standing committee when they are hearing evidence on the Bill.
Members should be aware that this Bill does not include any provisions for mandatory drug testing in the railway industry. However, it does include amendments to the Criminal Code with respect to the operation of railway equipment while impaired, as well as dangerous operation; the same rules that apply to us all in our cars, trucks, and boats.
Every one of us knows that it is a criminal offence to drink and drive, or to drive dangerously. The public has a right to expect that these prohibitions apply to the operation of trucks, airplanes, ships, and trains. While this true of the first three, many would be surprised and dismayed to know that criminal prosecution for those offences does not apply to persons responsible for the movement of railway equipment.
Railway Safety Act
This curious situation probably arose because railway companies own and control the railway equipment and the tracks over which it moves, employ the persons who operate the equipment, and even have their own police forces. A combination of railway operating rules and internal enforcement may have been the justification for an otherwise unacceptable omission.
The best known and long established rule in the railway industry is "Rule G" which states:
The use of intoxicants or narcotics by employees subject to duty, or their
possession or use while on duty, is prohibited.
This actual prohibition is more restrictive than that of the Criminal Code, which is only triggered after a threshold level of alcohol has been exceeded. "Rule G" has clearly been an effective measure in ensuring that alcohol or drugs do not constitute a hazard to safety. The record shows that few railway accidents have been attributed to the use of these substances. Nevertheless, railway operating employees work difficult hours and spend much of their time away from home. Research into use of alcohol and the increasing problem of drugs indicate that these working conditions create a high risk of substance abuse. Therefore, in developing the concepts for the railway safety Bill, it was clear that more was needed than only a company rule, albeit a largely effective one, to prevent the possible operation of trains while impaired.
Train crews are routinely responsible for the safety of several hundred passengers. They control the movement of freight trains valued at many millions of dollars which, to an increasing extent, include a wide variety of dangerous commodities. The public is exposed to the operation of trains throughout the country, not only as passengers or motorists at grade crossings, but as individuals living and working near railway lines. It is essential that train crews be alert on the job and that their vigilance be not in any way impaired by alcohol or drugs. For this reason, the Criminal Code provisions that apply to truck drivers, ships' captains, aircraft pilots, and to every motorist, should also apply to railway employees.
There are certain fundamental principles on which the regulation of railway safety in Canada must be based. As I stated earlier, safety regulation must be separated from responsibility for economic regulation, and further separated from accident investigation. The roles and responsibilities of the regulator and railway management must be clearly defined. The regulator must have the power to protect public and employee safety. Management must be responsible and accountable for the safety of operations. Consultation is essential, including full public inquiries on important issues. Regulation must be flexible and responsive in an environment of rapidly changing services and technology. Unnecessary and unproductive regulations should be eliminated, and penalties for offences must be meaningful.
The Bill before us has been drafted to deal with these many concerns. I will highlight the major aspects of the Bill which correct the deficiencies of the existing legislation and create a

February 4, 1988
Railway Safety Act
better legislative framework for the regulation of the railway industry.
This Bill provides a clear focus on safety by placing in a single Act all the federal Government's powers for the regulation of railway safety. Unlike the existing Railway Act, decision making under this Bill is concerned only with questions of safe rail operation which, by definition, includes the safety of the general public. By allocating those powers to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and leaving economic regulation of railways with the National Transportation Agency, the Bill will achieve that needed separation of responsibilities. The same separation will be achieved for accident investigation by the Transportation Accident Investigation Bill, soon to be tabled.
The Railway Safety Act will give the Government all the powers necessary to ensure safety on the railways. For the construction, maintenance, and operation of the system, the railways must satisfy the Minister that each element has been planned, executed, and controlled in a manner that is consistent with regulations and rules. The Act clearly makes the railways responsible for developing and implementing these measures and does not place the Minister, or government officials, in the position of making management decisions. The Minister will have the essential power to accept or reject management's proposals.
The Governor in Council will establish the basic regulations for the safety of the system, without limitation of the power to determine the content of those regulations. The Minister will have the power to impose rules of operation where railway companies have failed, for whatever reason, to develop rules which are acceptable and where these rules are essential for safe operation. The Minister will also the power to order companies to cease using, and to remove, structures whose existence pose a threat to safety.
These are extensive powers. In order to ensure that they are used effectively, the Bill provides for regular consultation by the creation of a railway safety consultative committee. The committee will comprise representation from the railways, railway unions and shippers, as well as persons having special interest or expertise in railway safety matters. This will create a forum for exchange of ideas and views, and a means to anticipate and solve problems in order that the proposed regulatory changes be carefully thought through. In this manner, the Minister can use consultation to avoid confrontation.
The anachronisms that exist in the Railway Act are the result of including detailed technical subjects in legislation. The railway safety Bill establishes the basis for effective regulation, leaving the determination of technical details to regulations and rules. It will not rapidly become outdated.
The vast majority of engineering work on Canada's railways is routine and repetitive. The new Bill will allow the regulator to designate those items of construction and alteration which cannot be undertaken without the express approval of the
Minister. By limiting procedures for other routine projects to selective filing of affidavits which attest to the safety of the completed work, a significant burden of unproductive regulation will be lifted from the Government. But the responsibility of railway management for safe operation will remain undiminished, while the powers of inspection under the Railway Safety Act will enable the Government to monitor the safety of any of these projects at any time.
MO)
Mr. Justice Foisy recommended that the government take steps to keep railway operating rules up to date. This Bill provides a streamlined rule change process which permits regulations and rules to incorporate other material by reference, including automatic update of that reference, and establishes time limits to encourage prompt decision making by the regulator. These provisions, along with the exemption of railway rules from review and publishing requirements of the Statutory Instrument Act will provide for the timely updating of the rules under which the railways operate.
The Foisy Commission also called for separation of rule making and accident investigation and for prosecution for breach of rules, both of which have been provided for in this Bill.
Finally, Mr. Justice Foisy recommended that railway legislation require the reporting of employee medical conditions which may jeopardize railway safety. Hon. Members will find this provision in Clause 35 of the Bill.
By dropping unnecessary and unproductive regulatory activities, and by simplifying and speeding up the evaluation and approval process, the Railway Safety Act will permit the redirection of existing resources into more productive areas.
Clearly, in today's environment, the emphasis must be on inspection for compliance, with the powers of inspection broadened to cover all disciplines, not just engineering. Regulatory staff can be placed anywhere on the system where they are needed. Inspectors appointed under the Railway Safety Act will have the full power to order railways to stop any operation that may prejudice safety.
Since this power could cause serious interruptions in railway operations, railway companies and shippers have concerns about the potential for unnecessary or, indeed, improper use. There will be no compromise on the ability of inspectors to issue these orders.
At the same time, however, the Bill requires the inspectors to do so through railway supervisory staff, unless this is impossible, and to notify the Minister when an order of this nature has been issued. The Minister will then be in a position to judge if these powers are being exercised as intended and will be able to rescind any order which is inappropriate.
I should like to bring to the attention of Hon. Members the penalty provisions of this Bill. Fines of up to $50,000 for corporations and up to $10,000 or imprisonment for up to one
February 4, 1988

year for individuals are created, along with the power to treat continued violations as separate punishable offences for each day incurred. These constitute meaningful penalties to any organization or individual. The railway safety Bill fills the gap that exists in the current legislation.
We have taken the opportunity presented by this Bill to create new powers for Government to protect the security of the system. Sadly, threats to security are an increasing problem world-wide, often with transportation systems as the target. Provisions were made in the Aeronautics Act to deal with security in the air. The railway safety Bill includes similar powers which will help the Government to react to such threats on the ground. While we hope that it will never be necessary to use these powers, it is essential that we create them now to protect the system in the future.
Finally, the railway safety Bill introduces a number of amendments to related legislation. Of particular importance are the amendments to the Criminal Code. As 1 noted earlier, these amendments will add railways to the list of modes which are subject to prohibitions against dangerous operation and operation while impaired. The Bill also repeals the Railway Relocation and Crossing Act, but retains and expands the essential powers of that legislation which allow the Government to promote improvements to safety.
The Bill before us was prepared after thorough consultation with provinces, municipalities, railways, railway unions, shippers, shippers of dangerous commodities, owners of private railway equipment, and of course public interest groups.
We received excellent co-operation and major contributions from all participants. While we believe that the provisions of the Bill have widespread support among the persons consulted, obviously not everyone got everything they wanted. I expect that we will have the opportunity to discuss any such concerns as the standing committee reviews the Bill.
As the Minister of Transport has said on every Bill which has been referred to a legislative or standing committee, if the committee after hearing the evidence has any amendments which can help the Bill and they are within any reasonable possibility, he is more than happy to accept them. Indeed, he has a history of accepting them. I think, in my experience here, that he has accepted more amendments to more Bills than any Minister with whom I have worked in this Government as well as in the previous Government.
Public perception of railway safety is conditioned overwhelmingly by the accidents in Mississauga, Flinton, and the train collisions of last month. These accidents have sensitized all of us to the potential dangers of any railway accident.
In his press conference after tabling the Bill, the Minister took the opportunity to reassure Canadians that our railways are basically safe. Moreover, progressively over the recent past, they have become safer. As I said earlier, in seven of the last eleven years, CP Rail has been the safest class one railway in North America. Over the same period, CN Rail has been
Railway Safety Act
consistently within the top six. This is a good record, which extends to include the smaller railway companies as well. It has been achieved and maintained at a time when the safety performance of all major North American railways has been improving.
The Government keeps a close watch on how the industry performs. As examples, over the period from 1979 to 1986, the total number of train accidents decreased by some 38 per cent, while fatalities decreased by 23 per cent and injuries by 16 per cent. What is more, the statistics for 1986 include the tragic number of deaths and injuries at Hinton. The latest results show no deterioration in this performance during 1987, even though railway freight traffic increased dramatically over levels in 1986.
While there have been major improvements in safety performance in 1986, still 116 persons died and 3,523 persons were injured in railway accidents. These numbers are unacceptably high, and we must act to reduce them. To do so requires an understanding of what is happening. Of the total fatalities, over 40 per cent are due to accidents at grade crossings and, almost without exception, these could have been prevented by the motor vehicle driver. Another 40 per cent of the fatalities include trespassers struck by moving train equipment. That was a figure which was much higher than 1 would have thought in my capacity as a layperson. Excluding 1986 and the Hinton collision, from 1979 to 1985 fatalities from train collisions and derailments have averaged two per year. In terms of injuries, 75 per cent of these involved employees, the vast majority being minor injuries sustained in performing duties and not related to accidents involving trains.
To place railway statistics in perspective, Hon. Members should be aware that while 116 persons lost their lives in railway related accidents during 1986, 90 people were fatally injured in aviation related accidents, 35 lost their lives in commercial shipping and fishing accidents, some 200 persons were killed in pleasure craft accidents on our waterways, and some 4,071 persons died on our roads. There is no room for complacency in respect of any mode of transportation. Any life lost is one too many. The message is that while railway safety can and will be improved, we are dealing with a controllable situation, not an industry in crisis.
While all Canadians are aware of major railway accidents, they are seldom as well informed about the follow-up. Our record is good. The Government established the Toronto area dangerous goods task force and the task force on the shipment of dangerous goods through the B.C. Lower Mainland. Both these groups have involved provincial and municipal Governments and have consulted widely throughout the areas under study. The task forces will be reporting to the Minister later this year on major questions surrounding the movement of dangerous goods through urban areas. The work has already provided insight into the risks and alternatives for transporting hazardous materials, and the results should be relevant for all communities throughout the country.

February 4, 1988
Railway Safety Act
As mentioned earlier, the Government quickly commissioned Mr. Justice Foisy to carry out a full investigation into the tragedy at Ffinton. You will recall that the Minister released Mr. Justice Foisy's very thorough report to the public and also made public the progress on implementing his recommendations. Members will be delighted to know that the railway safety Bill includes all of the legislative recommendations of Mr. Justice Foisy.
Significant changes have been made to rules governing areas of rest for trained crews. The unsatisfactory "deadman pedal" is now a thing of the past in mainline operations and will soon disappear from all locomotives, having been replaced by the more reliable and tamper proof reset safety control device.
Wherever possible, the recommendations of the Foisy report have already been implemented. Other longer term proposals are under active consideration. One example is Mr. Justice Foisy's conclusion that the advanced train control system holds great promise for improved railway safety. The Government agrees and, as I noted earlier, the Minister recently announced on behalf of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret), a $15 million program to support the development of this technology by the Canadian railway supply industry.
I have spoken of the terrible toll taken at our grade crossings. Members are probably aware of the Government's longterm program to assist provinces and municipalities in reducing these accidents. Funding has been made available for improving the safety of grade crossings by installation of warning lights, bells, and automatic barriers or by physical changes which will improve the safety of crossings.
A companion program has provided financial assistance for the construction of grade separations. It is encouraging to note that grade crossing injuries and fatalities have decreased radically in recent years. The federal Government's funding programs have played an important role in maintaining this trend.
Of equal importance is the joint federal-provincial Government and railway industry program called Operation Lifesav-er. Operation Lifesaver is devoted to educating the public about the dangers associated with railway lines and railway operations. Originally targeted at making drivers aware of the hazards of grade crossings, the program also has shown great promise in teaching school children that trespassing on railway property can lead to tragic results, as we have too often seen. The Minister is enthusiastic about the results of Operation Lifesafer and hopes to increase this essential educational activity.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, there are many areas in which the Government has acted to improve safety on our railways. While great progress has been made, much more remains to be done. The introduction of this Bill into the House is an important step in continuing and accelerating this work. While
the safety performance of our railways is good, there is a need for improvement and we are committed to seeing that changes are made. The Railway Safety Act is the means to achieve that objective, and I am sure that all Members of the House will assist by giving this Bill speedy passage.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in my place today to participate in debate on the Railway Safety Act. In making my comments today I cast my mind back to another transportation Bill, one of those listed by the Parliamentary Secretary as being marks of achievement by this Government and Ministers of Transport in the last two or three years, that is, Bill C-75, the Canada Shipping Act.
I recall that when that Bill was undertaken, circumstances were very similar. The Parliamentary Secretary has told the House about some of the current archaic provisions in legislation with respect to regulation of the railway; the minimal fines which are available under the current Act, and the fact that there are not provisions, for example, for someone operating equipment under the influence of alcohol because the Bill is literally many decades old. Any Bill has to be an improvement on something that was drafted in the 1940s.
I will, therefore, begin by acknowledging that any Bill which brings us into the 1980s and lifts us decades beyond the forties when the current legislation was drafted must be an improvement. However, having acknowledged that this is an improvement, I must say that I hope the Government will approach the Railway Safety Act with an attitude similar to that which was displayed during the course of debate and, in particular, in committee hearings on Bill C-75, the Canada Shipping Act. That Bill as well replaced a very old piece of legislation. It brought the Canada Shipping Act into the 1980s. It took account of modern technology and modern means of managing and operating shipping equipment.
When we dealt with that Bill the Government was open to amendments which would improve the first draft of the legislation. In fact, as I recall, there were 11 or 12 amendments made to Bill C-75 which I believe were substantive and important amendments. There was one very dramatic change made to Bill C-75 in that Clause 4 was dropped.
I hope that with regard to the Railway Safety Act the Government will show the same degree of interest in having the strongest possible Bill passed by Parliament and will not merely be satisfied with pointing to improvements made only because we are replacing a Bill which is decades old. It is very easy to give the appearance of making improvements when replacing a Model T with a 1980 Cadillac. We want to put forward the best legislation possible.
In examining the legislation we must ask ourselves why we are here today discussing the Railway Safety Act. What was the catalyst which brought us to this point? It is true that this legislation ought to be have been dealt with a long time ago. As a Liberal and a supporter of the former Government I can
February 4, 1988

say that it should have been dealt with by the former administration. That is an honest comment. However, now that we are dealing with the Bill, let us cast our mind back to the catalyst which seized the Government and the House of this issue.
More than anything it was the train derailment in Hinton, Alberta, on February 8, 1986, which took 23 lives that focused Parliament and the Ministry on the issue of railway safety. That derailment, coupled with the new transportation environment in Canada, namely, deregulation, is what focused this House on the issue of railway safety.
Two days after the Hinton derailment and the tragic loss of 23 lives the Ministry appointed the Foisy Commission to look into all aspects of railway safety and operations. We applauded the Minister for that then as we do now. Indeed, I think all Members of Parliament would agree that Judge Foisy produced an excellent piece of work, a thorough review of the operations of the railways in this country with particular emphasis on the regulations necessary for the safe operation of railways.
Upon looking at the Bill before us today one would have to agree that the vast majority of the recommendations of the Foisy Commission report, with a few exceptions, can be found in whole or in part within the provisions of Bill C-105. I say "in whole or in part" because there are a couple of areas which I believe are exceedingly important in which 1 believe the recommendations have not been implemented in the spirit in which they were intended by Judge Foisy. The primary concern of the Liberal Party with Bill C-105-and 1 would hope the Parliamentary Secretary would pay attention because he might want to consider amendments-is the whole notion proposed by the Government that there is finally to be a split between the economic regulation of the railways and the safety regulation of the railways. The Parliamentary Secretary has very clearly said today that a prime consideration for the Government, and in fact a prime recommendation of the Foisy Commission report, is that there be a split between those who are in charge of economic regulation of the railways and those who are in charge of the safety regulation of the railways, for obvious reasons.
If both responsibilities are contained within one agency, the NTA, there is a clear conflict of interest. There is a conflict between those concerned with the economics, the commercial aspect of railway operations, and those concerned with safety. The Government, quite rightly, and Mr. Justice Foisy, quite rightly, said that there must be a split of those responsibilities.
The Government is telling us that we have accomplished that split in this Bill because those responsible for safety regulation will be transferred from the NTA to the Ministry of Transport under the responsibility of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and there will no longer be a conflict of interest. That move takes a step in the right direction, but it does not
Railway Safety Act
fulfil the purpose the Parliamentary Secretary outlined when introducing this Bill today.
How can we possibly conceive of the notion that putting those responsible for safety regulation under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transport will solve the conflict of interest problem? After all, it is the Minister of Transport, as a matter of political policy, who has introduced deregulation in Canada. In the last year and a half, this is the Minister who has introduced the concept of deregulation in all modes of transport. He has abolished the independent nature of the CTC and has set up the NTA which takes directives from the Minister.
If there was a conflict of interest within the NTA because people making economic regulations and people making safety regulations were sitting in the same room, then surely to goodness there must be a conflict of interest when the Minister of Transport, who himself is the author of deregulation, is also the person responsible for safety. It is our belief that we have avoided one conflict of interest and have created another.
The Minister must now wear two hats. The primary proponent of and cheerleader for deregulation who is telling the railways to get lean and mean and to be competitive will, because of the provisions of this Bill, be the same gentleman who has responsibility for those people who will enact and enforce safety regulations. That is a conflict of interest for the Minister of Transport himself. I submit that it is perhaps a worse conflict than that which currently exists within the NTA.
I have raised this with the Parliamentary Secretary because I believe that when this goes to committee, we can develop amendments to the Bill that will ensure that the regulatory arm that operates under the jurisdiction of the Minister operates in some kind of quasi-independent manner. That is not specifically spelled out or clear in the Bill as it reads now. We do not know if a group of employees will be given a suite of offices down the hall from the Minister. We do not know if they will operate under the directive of the Minister on a daily, weekly and monthly basis. It is not clear, and as long as it remains unclear, the Minister of Transport, perhaps unwittingly, has been put into a terrible conflict by those who have drafted this piece of legislation.
On the one hand, the Minister will be telling the railways to compete, to cut costs, to make the operations lean and competitive, to be on an even footing with our friends south of the border in hauling traffic east and west, and on the other hand that they have to be safe. It is a difficult role for one single individual to play. That is why we recognized it as a conflict within the NTA. It is puzzling, then, why we would put the Minister in exactly the same conflict we wanted to avoid in the NTA itself.
That is one area of major concern to the Liberal Party. I say that with the knowledge that according to CTC figures, both CN Rail and CP Rail have cut their strength from a joint total of 88,478 employees in 1981 to 78,249 in 1985. If we had more

February 4, 1988
Railway Safety Act
recent figures, we would see that the cuts are even deeper. More than 10,000 people have been cut. The railways ascribe these cuts to technological change, and to some extent, I suppose that could be substantiated. However, the unions charge that many of these cut-backs have reduced safety by lowering inspection and maintenance standards.
We are living in an age of deregulation. One need only look South of the border where there has been 10 years of experience with deregulation, particularly on the air side, since 1978 and at what has happened to safety standards there to appreciate the enormous new pressures that will be on operators to function.
Bearing in mind this new conflict for the Minister and the Minister's ability to wear two hats, one as cheerleader for modernization and streamlining and the other as cheerleader for safety, I would like to bring to the attention of the House Clause 41 of the Bill, the offences clause. This clause provides that on indictment, in the case of a corporation like CN or CP, a fine of not exceeding $50,000 is payable. In the case of an individual, the fine is not to exceed $10,000 or imprisonment of one year. On summary conviction, the fine is $25,000 for the corporation and $5,000 for the individual.
When the Parliamentary Secretary introduced the Bill, he talked about existing regulations and said how silly they were. The maximum fine for a company was $100 and for an individual it was $8. He said that that needed to be upgraded. Well, this is the upgrade on the fines.
The maximum fine for an individual employee making $25,000 or $35,000 a year is $10,000 and the maximum fine for a billion-dollar corporation is $50,000. At a time when we expect these companies to cut their costs and to be mean, lean and competitive, the temptation to scrimp on safety expenditures and to cheat is stronger than ever. However, the maximum fine for a billion-dollar corporation is $50,000 and for an individual is $10,000. The fines and offences contained in Clause 41 are out of whack. We had exactly the same problem under the Canada Shipping Act which provided for fines which were ridiculously low.
1 suggest to the Parliamentary Secretary that this is another area we ought to explore in committee. We may be able jointly to come to some agreement on amendments. I say frankly to the Parliamentary Secretary that we cannot always assume the goodwill of individuals or corporations. That is why we provide for offences in law.
Frankly, when faced with the possibility of a maximum fine of $50,000-but it could be $5 or $50,000-for a safety offence or with a million-dollar cost for fixing a problem, some companies might decide that it would be cheaper to take a chance on a $50,000 fine than it would be to spend the funds necessary to solve the safety problems. I think this $50,000 fine, given the scheme of things-

It only takes one day to lose 23 lives, such as on February 8, 1986. In just one day many people can be killed. The fact it is $50,000 a day does not assure me that there is a satisfactory deterrent to the people operating our railways to try to cheat the system. I would like to see that number increased dramatically. I hope we can discuss this in committee and come to a mutually agreed upon sum and have this amended. We were able to do that with respect to a number of offences under the Canada Shipping Act by all-Party agreement. I would like the Parliamentary Secretary to take a note of that and give consideration to it.
There is another part of this Bill which I have some trouble with the way it is drafted. It concerns the railway safety consultative committee and Clause 44 of the Bill. There are five positions on the committee guaranteed for business, the railways and shippers. Four positions are at the discretion of the Minister. There is one position for labour. It seems to me that that committee is awfully heavily loaded in favour of the railways. Yes, they should be substantially represented, but not, I submit, overwhelmingly represented. I do not think one labour representative is an adequate voice to balance the competing and sometimes different views of the railways themselves.
Neither do I see a position on this committee for the public. What do I mean by the public? Many Members will remember the Mississauga spectacle of 1979 when 250,000 people had to evacuate their homes. No Party has a monopoly on virtue in its desire to prevent a repeat of that kind of incident. In fact, I see a member of the government Party who is frequently on his feet with respect to the transportation of dangerous and hazardous materials through populated centres. Yet it seems to me there has to be a provision for a public group on the committee, someone with a non-vested interest. There should be an opportunity for the public's voice to be heard; those who live in communities where dangerous and hazardous materials are shipped on a regular basis should have a direct say in this committee. I submit to the Parliamentary Secretary that this is an oversight which I hope can be corrected when we get to committee stage.
There is an organization in Toronto which arose out of the Mississauga derailment of 1979 called M-Track. That group has played the role of a public advocate on a regular basis, dealing with the speed of trains, the kind of material being moved, the way the material is secured. That kind of voice needs to be heard on the committee. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will agree that this is an amendment we must make. I hope as well he will give consideration to the weighting of the committee. Surely, as presently constituted, it will not lead to an effective and well-functioning committee.
There were a couple of recommendations made by Mr. Justice Foisy in his excellent report which are not found in this
February 4, 1988

Bill. One of those is the notion that there ought to be, in addition to the technology now in place, an oral notification of train meets by radio. I understand there has been consultation between the unions, the companies, the regulators, and a general agreement that the recommendation, while made with Mr. Justice Foisy's best judgment, is not one that would contribute to safety. We accept that that recommendation is not found in the Bill. However, there is a second recommendation covering hours of work scheduling. Again, we understand the Government is in a difficult position because in talking about work scheduling, you are talking about the collective bargaining process. Until some of those issues have been resolved at the bargaining table, it is difficult for Government to impose, in essence, part of the contract through legislation. However, I would note that recommendation and hope that the Government intends, when it is appropriate and the parties have come to some resolution of the question, to come back and amend the legislation at a later date.
I have tried in these remarks to raise a number of areas where I believe the Bill can be improved. These are matters to which members of all Parties should be able to lend their support. I now want to come back to the primary concern I have about the Bill, and its primary motivation which, as the Parliamentary Secretary rightly says, is the notion of setting up a separate, independent safety organization within the Department of Transport.
Currently the economic and safety regulators are in the same offices. That gives rise to at least a potential of a conflict of interest. The Government says it is going to solve that by moving the safety regulators away from the economic regulators. Yet they have been put in the office of the Minister of Transport, and that puts the Minister in an even worse situation of conflict of interest. On the one hand he is the proponent of the regulation, and on the other he is responsible for safety because there is no quasi independent agency.
It was very illuminating that in the Standing Committee on Transport a few days ago we had Mr. Barbeau, the Assistant Deputy Minister for Surface Transportation in the Department of Transport, and we asked him questions about the Foisy report and this Bill. We were concerned specifically with the question of whether or not we were splitting economic regulation from safety regulation. Here is what he said:
A second element was recommended by Justice Foisy, and that is the split between accident investigation and safety regulation. Again, the new Bill will do this in part. What is happening with the new Bill is that we are splitting off safety regulation from economic regulation, which now remains with the National Transportation Agency, and then in a Bill that will be introduced in the House some time soon, we hope, there will be further split between regulation and accident investigation.
Introducing a multimodal accident investigation board through a new Bill, after the fact, will not permanently resolve the problem of safety regulation in this country.
Railway Safety Act
While this Bill generally enjoys the support in principle of the Liberal Official Opposition, until amendments are made to the railway safety consultative committee, until amendments are made to reflect proper fines for offences by corporations, and until there is a proper separation of economic regulation and safety regulation so the Minister is out of the conflict of interest in which this Bill would place the Minister, we cannot endorse it as now drafted.
We have had experience with transportation matters in the past of seeing the House work as a cohesive unit, putting aside partisanship, and delivering good legislation. If the Minister and his Parliamentary Secretary accept my remarks in the spirit in which they have been given, 1 hope that we will produce a good Bill at the end of a proper and thorough investigative process at the committee stage.
I equally say to the Parliamentary Secretary that without some of these fundamental matters being addressed, the Bill will not get the kind of timely passage that at least in concept and principle it deserves.

Mr. Speaker, we are finally seeing some movement on legislation which has been called for at least since the mid 1940s. During the years that my colleagues and 1 have been here, and prior to that when former colleagues in the CCF and NDP were here, our Party annually called for this kind of legislation.
I recall being with the railway between the mid 1940s and early 1960s, and going to union meetings where this matter was discussed every time we met. Union officers would recite how they made repeated efforts with the railroads and the Government of the day to get a national railway safety Act. It is unfortunate that it has taken so long for Governments to see the light.
The NDP recognizes the urgent need for railway safety legislation. We will do all we can to assist in passing the legislation, hopefully in an amended way to make it even stronger.
I believe the motives of all Members from all Parties in the House will be above suspicion when it comes to dealing with safety, about which we all say there should be no compromise.
Bill C-105 represents the first opportunity Parliament has had to consider legislation responding not only to the Foisy report, which was released over a year ago, but responding to many other demands in this area. We are all aware of the rash of rail accidents in recent weeks, in which lives were lost. Of course, it is these types of accidents that make national headlines even though many more people are killed at railway crossings and in highway mishaps. Highway mishaps and railway crossing accidents do not attract as much attention as train wrecks or plane crashes, and I suspect that has made the public and the legislators complacent about other areas of safety.

February 4, 1988
Railway Safety Act
I agree with some of the remarks of my colleague from the Official Opposition. We are in a type of vacuum at the moment. The Government's headlong rush into deregulation before the implementation of all these other measures has left us a situation in which the CTC and the Rail Transport Committee of the CTC have ceased to exist as of December 31, while the new National Transportation Agency is still be reorganized after coming into place January 1. Many of the employees of the CTC are going to the new National Transportation Agency and the Department of Transport, and others are probably retiring early. In the meantime, the regulating authority for the devising of regulations, enforcing of regulations and the investigation of mishaps is spread throughout the NTA and the Department.
Over two years ago we pleaded with the Government not to implement Bill C-18 and Bill C-19 until all the accident and investigation boards were in place and the highway, railway, marine and air safety codes with their respective agencies were established. Even the Canadian Truckers Association pleaded with the Government, both privately and in appearances before the Transport Committee, to delay the implementation of Bill C-19 for at least a year, preferably two years, until the new national highway safety codes were in place with the jurisdictions that have control over highway traffic. The Government refused to listen.
Officials of the Department were present at a committee hearing on January 16. I asked: "With the National Transportation Agency being responsible for the devising and promulgating of regulations, until such time as a national accident investigation board is set up that covers rail, air, marine, whatever, who will be responsible?" I went on to say: "This may take another year or two before all this happens. In the meantime, who is responsible for the regulatory regime for investigations, inspections, enforcement and all the things that go with the regulations that will be in place?"
The answer I received was: "There are really three things going on with the creation of the National Transportation Agency with the Bill. The whole question of rail safety, including both the regulation of rail safety and accident investigation function has been left with the National Transportation Agency as it presently stands". The answer goes on: "The reason is there is no way the responsibility for railway safety can be transferred, for example, to Transport Canada without a piece of legislation". He went on to say that this brings into play the proposed Railway Safety Act. As soon as it is proclaimed, then the responsibility for railway safety will come over to Transport Canada with the function of accident investigation. It is all a matter of timing. As soon as the National Transportation Accident Investigation Act is proclaimed, the responsibility for action and investigation will then be split off from Transport Canada into the new agency. He ended up by saying: "It is a matter of things falling into place one after the other".
That sort of proves what I said two years ago, and several times since then, with respect to the Government's headlong rush into deregulation before having these three things in place. Now the scramble is on. The best I can say for the Government is that it is better late than never. However, the Government could have avoided a lot of the difficulties that have been there, presently are there, and will continue to be there for at least another number of months, if not a year or two. In fact, on January 19 the Atlantic district director of the National Transportation Agency, Rail Safety Branch, who chaired a meeting in Halifax, admitted that there is at present no agency empowered to investigate accidents or make other inquiries into matters related to railway safety. He said that rail safety in this country is in a state of flux. He is sure right about that.
I suppose we could give the Government some credit for trying to clean up the mess it made. People should have to clean up their own mess. Bill C-105 is an attempt to allow some sort of regulation to be put in place to deal with what is quickly becoming a critical situation.
We have to look at this Bill to see what it does for rail safety and we find that by itself it does not do very much. The most important provision in this Bill gives the Government the power to pass regulations having to do with the safe operations of railways, but by itself this Bill does not provide for high standards of safe railway operating practice. There are no specifications for adequate frequency of inspections. There are no specifications for maintenance of track and equipment. Therefore, by itself the Bill does little for safety. It just legislatively allows someone else to do it.
Much will depend on what regulations the Government passes following the passing of this legislation. I feel that the legislation should contain some general and specific principles in each area of maintenance, inspection, investigation and enforcement so that there are some firm legislative requirements put upon those who draft regulations and enforce them and those who carry out inspections and investigations and enforce their findings.
I hope the Government will at some point present to the House a draft of its proposed safety regulations pertaining to Bill C-105. If it does not, perhaps it would consider-and I ask the Parliamentary Secretary to raise this matter with the Minister-to at least give a draft of the proposed regulations to the standing committee so that we can look at it while dealing with the Bill and while we are hearing from witnesses. In fact, I have been on the Standing Committee on Transport for 20 years next June and I believe the standing committee could be very helpful to the Minister and to the industry in drafting those regulations. My advice is to make available to the Standing Committee on Transport, if not to all Members of the House, the substance of the Government's proposed regulations so that the committee can make its recommendations as well.
February 4, 1988

Some amendments to this Bill are necessary. The Bill as it is tabled is vague in a number of instances. I depicted the Bill as very nebulous. 1 do not know whether the Minister is out in space or spaced out with the nebuli. For example, Section 4 defines a number of terms introduced in the Act. One troublesome definition is for relevant associations or organizations of persons employed by a railway company. The Act says the Minister must declare by order that a particular union is a relevant association or organization. I thought that was something that the Canada Labour Relations Board did. All the railway brotherhoods, as far as 1 know, are certified as railway employees by the Canada Labour Relations Board. I do not know why the Minister needs to have an additional authority to pick and choose which union he things is a relevant association or organization. We already know who they are.
The wording of this section of the Act could lead to some very interesting confrontations if it is left as it is now written. The Minister could leave some railway unions out of the consultation provided for in the Bill. If that is not asking for trouble, 1 do not know what is.
The Government does not seem to have considered employees very carefully when it drafted the Bill. That is why the railway safety consultative committee the Bill creates is structured so unfairly. We are just fed up with the unfairness of this Government in so many ways since September 4, 1984, and it continues to perpetuate unfairness in its legislation. The proposed make-up of the Bill betrays the Government's intention to allow railways to regulate themselves with minimal interference from the Government. The Minister will be represented on the committee by as many as five members. The railways will be represented by five members. The railway employees will be represented by only one. It specifies the Canadian Railway Labour Association in the Act. What if the railway brotherhoods do not want a representative from the Canadian Railway Labour Association? What is the Minister going to do then? Will he just barrel ahead anyway? That is no way to treat the 50,000 or 60,000 people engaged in the operation of railways in Canada.
This kind of set-up effectively stacks the deck against labour in any dispute that might arise in the committee. Perhaps that is what the Government wants. That is not the only example in this Bill of the Government trying to make life easier for the railway companies. Clause 11, for example, takes the responsibility to ensure that some railway works are safe from government regulators and gives the responsibility to the companies. This will no doubt make life easier for the companies, but what it does for safety is a mystery to me.
Perhaps the Government has good reasons to want to help the rail companies through some pretty rough times since both CN an CP are in a much weaker competitive position, thanks to deregulation. However, safety has to be a primary concern. It cannot be sacrificed or compromised. When a company is victimized by the bottom line syndrome under deregulation, and is faced with competing modes of transportation, and
Railway Safety Act
when American railroads have a licence to raid up to $2 billion of the revenues of CN or CP in any year, otherwise honest and reputable corporations are forced into a position where they have to cheat. They have to cut corners. They have to save every nickel they can find.
The Bill is too soft on the rail companies. It comes down hard on employees in some ways, especially in terms of the setting out of offences and the establishment of penalties for contravening the legislation. There is a relatively small difference between the penalties faced by corporations and those faced by individuals. Ten thousand dollars is a great deal of money to an individual who, as my colleague said earlier, might be making $25,000, $30,000 or $50,000 per year. A $50,000 penalty placed on a corporation which has revenues of anywhere from $1 billion to $3 billion per year, depending on how good a year it is, amounts to nothing more than a licence fee to be unsafe. I submit that the fine and the penalty should be severe enough that they are equal to or exceed the cost of the safe practices which should have been carried out before a penalty was imposed.
This type of unfairness cannot be tolerated. The penalties on the railroads should be at least 10 times as high, up to $500,000. Safety costs money. A company which has been unsafe or which has carried out an unsafe practice should be required to pay more money than it would have cost to implement a safety measure. If that were in the legislation, then the railroads would be not only more mindful but they would know that this is one area in which they cannot and do not dare cut corners or slow down especially in matters concerning maintenance and inspections. We hope that the Government will agree to accept changes in this area as well.
The fact that an individual not only can be fined but can go to prison for neglecting to tell his or her physician that he or she holds a certain kind of job with the railroad while a corporation found guilty of a flagrant violation of the Bill causing loss of life and damage to property has to pay only what amounts to small change is an imbalance of some proportion.
Clause 35 of the Bill threatens the confidentiality between patient and physician. Physicians are required to provide confidential medical information to railway employers rather than to the Minister or to the regulatory agency. How can the employer be prevented from abusing this information?
Drug and alcohol testing are not specifically mentioned in Bill C-105, but it allows for regulations governing the control or prohibition of the consumption of alcoholic beverages and the use of drugs. In other words, the Minister will be able to allow companies to administer drug and alcohol tests to its employees. There are a few points about that issue which need to be remembered.
First, drug testing will not prevent accidents or abuse. The Bill is silent on preventive and non-punitive approaches to

February 4, 1988
Railway Safety Act
alleged problems of drugs and alcohol in the workplace. The Bill could have included, and 1 hope it will, provisions to improve employee assistance programs.
I want to recommend to all Members an article that was in this morning's issue of The Globe and Mail. It appeared on the editorial page and is written by Professor Brian Tucker of the University of Saskatchewan. It is entitled: "Stress rides the rails". It is not only those who ride the rails, locomotive engineers, brakemen and conductors, but those who hold a number of other high stress positions which exist in railway operations. I think particularly of train dispatchers in this regard.
I can recall a senior life insurance executive telling me a number of years ago that insurance companies would rather insure the fellow who paints the Lions Gate Bridge or washes windows on a 50 storey building than insure a train dispatcher or an air traffic controller. The difference in mortality rates and disability rates was remarkable. I have seen people in those occupations who are faced with stomach ulcers, nervous breakdowns and heart attacks when they are at the age of 40, 45 or 50. These people a number of years ago had an average life expectancy of 56 compared to the national average a number of years ago of about 72.
The whole area of stress includes as well other personal, mental and physical problems. A person in these sensitive positions has to be vigilant. They are highly trained, competent and conscientious people. It is not just alcohol or drug use or abuse that causes stress. In fact, it is my view that the rate of alcohol use or abuse or drug use or abuse among employees in those types of jobs on the railroads and the airlines is far less than among the public generally in most other occupations.
If there is any one thing that one is conscious of when one is working on a railroad, for example, is "Rule G". An employee to whom this rule applies does not consume alcohol when on duty or subject to duty. That is drilled into one's head from the first day on the job. One is reminded of it continually not only by supervisors but by fellow employees. They know that the lives and property of thousands of other people are in their hands.
1 recommend this article by Professor Tucker and other studies that have been done to Hon. Members. The legislation should provide for, and require, sufficient funding for employee assistance plans. I am confident that in this respect the full co-operation of the employees and of their unions will be obtained. The federal Government and the railroads should share in the funding of these types of programs.
It is unsafe to send a man to work to run a locomotive or dispatch trains when he is having severe difficulties at home. Those problems are on his mind when he should be concentrating on his work. Dealing with this is called risk management. Without those types of programs being carried out and a requirement in the law there is not sufficient risk management.
I wish to point out a regrettable omission in the Bill. In Bill C-105 there is no protection given to railway employees who report unsafe practices or conditions to the Minister or to a regulatory agency. The Bill can be improved by adding a provision which states that an employee cannot be dismissed because of disclosures of unsafe practices and conditions to authorities outside of railway management. It is called whistle blowing, if Hon. Members will pardon the expression, on the railway.
I remember a train wreck near the station where I was working in Saskatchewan. The section foreman had won the prize for the best section in the whole Medicine Hat Division. He had received merit marks, awards, certificates on several occasions and even a handshake from the General Manager of Western Lines on several occasions. He was a man from Czechoslovakia who escaped that country in 1939. All his life in Canada he worked on the CPR rails, on the tracks. He became a section foreman, a very good one. The investigation showed that that mishap was due to a broken rail. Who received 35 demerit marks and was taken out of service for two weeks? That section foreman. Several times a year, year in and year out, that section foreman would plead with the roadmas-ter, the division engineer, and write to the superintendent of the division, pleading and asking for some more rails, or some newer rails, if not new ones. He knew the track and he knew what the rails were like. He could not get them; it cost too much money. Because he was doing a conscientious job, even though he had the best section in the whole Medicine Hat Division, he is the one who was made the scapegoat. The railway management did not even receive a slap on the wrist from the Canadian Transport Commission.
We have had reports given to us of a carman "bad ordering" a car, and his supervisor takes the "bad order" tag off and says to leave it on the train. If the carman objects, he is considered to be insubordinate and a trouble-maker, so he keeps his mouth shut. But there is an unsafe practice going on. Trying to document something like that is next to impossible.
The regulations have to include some procedures that protect the employee on the ground on the job, and protect the employee in his employment if and when he blows the whistle on unsafe practices by railway management. That is a must. It is not that the employee wants to get even with the company or get even with some foreman or superintendent; it is because the safety regulations require them, as well as him, to operate safely and carry out their duties in order that the railway operation be more safe.
I wish to say to the Parliamentary Secretary through you, Mr. Speaker, that it will require the help and the maximum co-operation of 50,000 to 60,000 railway employees for this to work to its maximum best. To pay so little attention to their conditions, and to have some unfair provisions in there, will not generate their co-operation and assistance. It will only worsen morale further and make bad attitudes worse.
February 4, 1988

I hope that the consultative committee is given a little muscle. The employees' representation on it should at least be equal to-I submit that it should be larger-than the representation by the railroads. The railroads continually have the ear of the Minister. They continually have the ear of the National Transportation Agency. The employees do not. When they did, they did not get very far.
There are a couple of other things that are or will lead to further unsafe conditions. I have mentioned stress and fatigue, and physical and mental problems of an employee and the help that they need and deserve. That should be funded jointly by the railroads and the federal authority. But there are a couple of other things. The Parliamentary Secretary stated that the Railway Crossing Act is repealed and will be covered in this Bill, if 1 heard him correctly. I do not know the figures, but over the years thousands of people have been killed at railway crossings. Our country runs approximately 30 years behind European countries in the situation that we have with railway crossings, compared to them.
To maximize railway safety and safety to the public, something has to be done about level crossings. It will cost money. 1 estimate a minimum cost of SI00 million a year for six to ten years to really do something about level crossings. There are thousands of locations where flashing red lights and the arms across the track are not sufficient. There will have to be an overpass or an underpass. The last one that was done in Regina cost $11 million, but it is a beautiful job. Six lanes of traffic move under the double track main railway line. It was jointly funded by the federal, provincial, and municipal Governments. That has to continue, and it has to be substantially increased. The funds are woefully inadequate. It is a disgrace.
There are more than 100,000 level crossings in this country, some of which could be completely done away with. For example, there are areas on the Prairies where a crossing every mile is not needed. In many areas one every two miles would be fine. But it would mean that a road would have to be built parallel to the track for that extra mile in order to do away with one crossing. There is an area where rail safety can be substantially enhanced when we start removing tens of thousands of level crossings and replacing them with overpasses or underpasses, grade separations as they are called.
I want you to visualize, Mr. Speaker, an 80-car freight train of grain moving from Moose Jaw to Assiniboia. On the Prairies there are thousands of farm fuel trucks owned by oil companies or contractors delivering fuel to farmers all over the three prairie provinces. In every location each truck makes a dozen or two dozen trips a day. They cross railway tracks a dozen or two dozen times a day. Visualize this, Mr. Speaker. It is still dark or it is getting dark, and that 80-car train of grain from Assiniboia to Moose Jaw-I will bring it the other way around in the right direction-ploughs into that farm fuel truck. The locomotive bursts into flames. The consist of the train is on the locomotive. The only communication that the train has beyond that locomotive is in the locomotive. Who is
Railway Safety Act
going to phone whom about what? If there are any carloads of dangerous goods on the train, who knows where they are? The locomotive is in flames, and it is miles from nowhere. Do you know why, Mr. Speaker, there is no one to do anything? The cabooses are going to be taken off. There will be no cabooses.
I find that the most incredible decision of the Canadian Transport Commission that I have ever seen, and they have made some dandy messes that contribute to unsafe practices. No matter what the railroads say about saving money-Mr. Speaker, I would like to have a few extra minutes, if I may have permission of the House after three o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member has two minutes left in his speech. Would the Hon. Member prefer to complete it now, if the House wishes?
Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank my colleagues. I will wind up quickly by referring to some things the Bill should do but does not do. It is nebulous. It is too vague. It is not strong enough in terms of what it requires of the railroads. It is unfair in terms of what it does with, for and to employees. Too many things are not in it that should be in it.
I hope the Parliamentary Secretary meant what he said about the Minister being willing and amenable to changes and improvements to the legislation. I hope that he is right and that he will forgive me for being a little bit doubtful, since of the 130 amendments moved to Bill C-18 and Bill C-19 I think the Government accepted 7 or 8 of them. Big deal. They were mostly ones dealing with minor details, but on the ones that really meant something, government Members sat there like sheep. Some of them even agreed with some of my amendments, but they sat there like sheep and followed their marching orders. So much for the independence of the committee.
My Party supports the railway safety Bill in principle, for we have been calling for such legislation for many years. We are sad that the Bill is so deficient, but we appreciate that it is a long overdue first try.
We will all be groping around in terms of what more we can do, but I think we could make that effort in committee. I plead with the Parliamentary Secretary to prevail upon the Minister to make available to us a draft, no matter how rough or incomplete, of regulations they are envisioning bringing in. The committee can be very helpful. We can hear the views of witnesses as well, which will make it even more useful in the finalizing of the new regulations.
Again I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the extra time. I hope the Bill will receive the many more improvements it so badly needs.

February 4, 1988
