subsubtopic: PRE-SCREENING OF CLAIMANTS-NEWSPAPER REPORT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday The Globe and Mail reported on a confidential government memorandum which, unfortunately, outlined the Government's true agenda on refugee applications, namely, to utilize the pre-screening stage Bill C-55 to eliminate nearly two-thirds of all claimants. In doing so the Government is revealing a very diabolical and despicable streak.
For months the two Ministers of Immigration have stated that the Bill contains no pre-screening at all. Yet, at the very same time, they are designing, in secret, a strategy that is based purely on the opposite, on pre-judging applications. The Government's intent is to maximize the efficiency of the system by indiscriminately keeping people from ever accessing the system. This is paramount to a hospital turfing out needy patients in the name of achieving greater efficiency.
I call upon the Government to abandon its deceitful calculations and to end its wishful role of trying to play both judge and jury. It should instead establish an independent process to judge these claims fairly and honestly, and provide Canadians with policies which they can respect and trust.

Mr. Speaker, the Government is leading the Canadian economy into the 21st century despite the incredible debt left by the Liberals. In the four years prior to 1984 spending grew by 15 per cent per year, effectively mortgaging the next generation. The interest payments on this debt amount to 30 cents of every dollar of federal revenue.
The Government has reduced the annual deficit from a high of $38 billion in 1984 to an estimated $29 billion this year, which represents the first consecutive three-year decline in 30 years. Yet the Opposition continually calls for increased public
spending, not caring about the long-term damage this will cause.
The Government has responded to Canadian needs with initiatives like the Special Grains Program and the National Day Care Strategy in a responsible manner, while the Opposition asks Canadian taxpayers to spend even more. Just think, Mr. Speaker, how huge the deficit would be if either opposition Party were allowed to implement its irresponsible spending plans.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and his Cabinet take every opportunity to protest the independence of standing and legislative committees. Too often, however, these protestations simply hide reality. We have just had another example of this in the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
As you know, Bill C-92 was referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture instead of to a legislative committee. There is a serious flaw in Bill C-92, a Bill to amend the Wheat Board Act, which flaw government members on the committee recognized. Despite this recognition, the majority members of the committee were unwilling to recommend any changes to the Bill without the approval of the Minister. You have guessed it, Mr. Speaker, the Minister gave the government members their marching orders-there are no amendments.
The Bill will be reported to the House to allow producer car rebates without recognition of the cost of those cars to the grain moving system. This, Mr. Speaker, is not the way parliamentary reform was supposed to operate.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-CONGRESSIONAL VOTE AGAINST FURTHER FUNDING FOR CONTRA FORCES IN NICARAGUA

speechtext:
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the American House of Representatives for giving peace a chance in Central America. Yesterday, the United States House, by a vote of 219 to 211, turned down the President's request to provide further military funds to the Contra rebels in Nicaragua.
The President's paranoic policy with respect to Nicaragua is totally wrong. It is an unwarranted, illegal interference by a superpower in the internal affairs of a small, poor country. It is a failure to recognize the principle of self-determination and it is a distortion of the real situation in that country. Nicaragua is not and never was a threat to the United States.
Finally, the President's policy was contrary to and undermined the peace plan agreed to by all Central American countries on the initiative of President Arias of Costa Rica, an initiative for which he won the Nobel Peace Prize. This is a good day for Central America and a good day for peace.

subtopic: OMISSION OF RIGHTS OF UNBORN BABIES
OMISSION OF RIGHTS OF UNBORN BABIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, where is our country heading? For many generations Canadians endeavoured to make laws in harmony with Holy Writ, but now our laws have to conform to the Charter of Rights, a document in which we had to fight to even get the name of God mentioned, a document that leaves out property rights and, even worse, makes no mention at all of the rights of unborn babies.
We lost the Sabbath Day as we knew it for many years because it did not conform to the Charter. Now we have abortion on request and unborn babies can be butchered in the womb simply as a birth-control measure. To our shame, we now let the convicted murderers live and permit the murder of unborn babies. It is enough to bring tears to the eyes of the Statue of Justice that stands silently in front of the Supreme Court of Canada.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-MINING EXPLORATION ACTIVITIES IN STRATHCONA PARK
BRITISH COLUMBIA-MINING EXPLORATION ACTIVITIES IN STRATHCONA PARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to call the attention of the House to a proposal of the B.C. Government to expand mining in Strathcona Park. The Government has changed provincial park boundaries to allow extended mining and exploration activity in the park.
Exploration activities by Cream Silver Mines Ltd. will lead to further mining in the park. Serious danger of contamination and destruction of major salmonid enhancement projects in the Great Central Lake and the Oyster River systems are a definite potential.
We in the NDP demand that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) use their powers under the Fisheries Act to suspend any further exploration and mining in Strathcona Park, to launch an in-depth investigation of the potential damage to fisheries systems in that park, and to hold public hearings to ascertain the wishes of the public in this matter.

Mr. Speaker, it now seems that the federal Government is renegotiating with the Province of Newfoundland for the abandonment of the Newfoundland Railway. This was negotiated before, but the parties could not reach an agreement that the Province of Newfoundland would accept.
Now it seems the province will accept an agreement. If the province is satisfied with it, I wish it well. However, I wish this agreement had been negotiated in public and not behind closed doors.
When the Terms of Confederation were brought forward in 1949, Newfoundlanders were promised a link with the mainland which would extend from North Sydney to Port aux Basques. 1 assume the people of Port aux Basques will be looked after by the Province of Newfoundland in the settlement with the federal Government. However, I do not want the federal Government to forget the obligation it took upon itself in the negotiations for the town of North Sydney and for the workers of Marine Atlantic. I would suggest to the federal Government that it treat the people of North Sydney fairly.

Mr. Speaker, in yesterday's editorial, the Globe and Mail reported the most shocking scandal we have known in the past 25 years, one that has an impact on Canadians today and will go on affecting us for the next 25 years. During the lengthy Liberal reign over this country, when the Liberals were unfortunately often supported by members of the Socialist Party, this country was spending money left and right, getting involved in frivolous expenditures and then having to borrow to buy the groceries.
That is why today, Canada has the largest per capita debt in the world. Canada ranks second after the United States in terms of absolute figures. We owe $172 billion abroad, that is, half the U.S. debt, for a country with one-tenth the population of the U.S. Mr. Speaker, that is a legacy we received from the Liberal big spenders. Lest we forget, the present Liberal
Leader was there at the time, with his present team, and they were there thanks to the Socialist Leader's support.
Something to think about for Canadians, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: ETHIOPIA-THREATENED FAMINE-NEED FOR UNIMPEDED ACCESS TO HUNGRY POPULATION
ETHIOPIA-THREATENED FAMINE-NEED FOR UNIMPEDED ACCESS TO HUNGRY POPULATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin on behalf of all my colleagues in the NDP caucus by joining with the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) in celebrating the vote in Congress last night on funding for the Contras. I would like to express my regret that the Canadian Government could not show as much distance from the policy of President Reagan as obviously a majority of U.S. Congressmen were willing to do; 1 suppose they are anti-American, too.
Let us turn our attention to another country torn not only by war but by famine, the country of Ethiopia. Many of us are disturbed by persistent reports that indicate food relief is being used as a political weapon by the Ethiopian Government. The problem of safe passage for emergency food supplies is of increasing concern. In that respect 1 draw attention to an allParty motion passed in the West German Bundestag calling for safe passage of those supplies. It specified that the impending famine must not be misused for political or military objectives; that the international humanitarian aid agencies must be guaranteed free and unhindered access to the needy population in all parts of Ethiopia; that relief convoys must be identifiable as such and it must be possible to check that they are not being misused for military purposes; and that food assistance and logistic support must not be misapplied for forced resettlement and villagization programs, nor misappropriated for the Ethiopian Army.
Those are the kinds of concerns on which we need a response from the Government. I hope the Minister in charge of this program will soon make a statement with respect to these charges and the effect they have on Canadian policy in that area.

subtopic: SUPREME COURT DECISION-OPPORTUNITY TO ENACT NEW HUMAN LIFE ACT
SUPREME COURT DECISION-OPPORTUNITY TO ENACT NEW HUMAN LIFE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, seen in positive terms, the Supreme Court decision on abortion now gives Parliament an historic opportunity to enact a comprehensive new statute, one that we might call the Human Life Act.
A Human Life Act would deal not only with abortion, genetic engineering, surrogate motherhood, and new forms of reproductive technology, but also euthanasia, suicide, and similar instances of intentional intervention in the human life cycle.
Oral Questions
The Human Life Act should provide a legal framework within which particular decisions can then be reached by the individuals concerned and their medical doctor.
The sanctity of human life makes it appropriate to deal with all these questions as variations on a single theme, even though the medical procedures and individual circumstances vary dramatically.
My hope is that we can move beyond the current level of debate and analysis of this subject by placing the abortion issue in this broader context of a full-field concern for human life.

Railway Safety Act

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-105, an Act to ensure the safe operation of railways and to amend certain other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport.

Mr. Speaker, in resuming debate on Bill C-105 I would like to say, having listened to the debate that has taken place, that the important thing to note is that we are in complete agreement. It is an essential Bill and important to Canadians. In the debate so far much information has been given, and in my brief remarks I want to touch on two main areas of the Bill because I believe all Canadians should know what is included in the Bill.
With respect to railway construction, Part 1 of the Bill establishes the Government's powers and procedures related to construction and alteration of railway works. Under this part of the Bill the Governor in Council will have unlimited power to make regulations which establish standards for these activities. Equally important is the fact that through this provision the Bill makes it possible for the Government to select which construction and alteration projects it wishes to evaluate in detail. As a result, for the first time the regulator can focus on projects which may affect the safety of railway operations or may cause concern to the general public. There will no longer be a requirement to process a multitude of project approvals which have little or no bearing on safety.
The Governor in Council will also be empowered to designate kinds of railways works which cannot be undertaken without the proposer, in most cases a railway company, giving prior notice to persons who may be affected. The Bill makes full provision for any objections to be considered before a decision is made to allow the work to proceed. By putting the onus on the railways to notify potential objectors, the Bill removes the burden of ensuring public input which is now placed on Government by the existing Railway Act.
Bill C-105 creates three categories of construction and alteration projects for regulatory purposes. I would like to comment on those. First, projects which must have ministerial approval before work can begin. Second, works which may be undertaken without ministerial approval provided no objections are received but for which an affidavit certifying the safety of the completed work must be filed with the Minister. Third, projects which may be carried out without reference to the regulator.
The first category of works includes projects for which engineering standards have been prescribed and which depart from those standards or those which meet standards but are
objected to by other persons on the grounds of safety. Section 10 of the Bill sets forth the procedures to be followed in seeking authority to proceed. The Minister may seek advice, hold an inquiry into the proposal, and must consider legitimate objections before rendering a decision. The bottom line is that the Minister has the necessary power to deny authority to proceed if he or she, as the case may be, is not satisfied with the proposal on the grounds of safety.
The Minister will not be placed in the position of ordering the proposing party to proceed with the project or to carry out the project in a certain manner. It is up to the proposer and, as usual, the railway company concerned, to come up with a plan that satisfies the Minister's requirements. If a railway company uses the rejection of a proposed work by the Minister as a reason to abandon the service, appeals for restoration or service may be made to the National Transportation Agency on the grounds of public convenience.
I should add, with the introduction in this House of Bill C-18 and Bill C-19, steps the Government has taken we are continuing with Bill C-105 to complete and complement the work already done.
Members should note that the Bill creates an assessment period of 60 days within which the Minister must advise the proposing party that their request is approved, rejected, or that more information is required. The Minister may extend the assessment period indicating the length of time of the extension and the reasons for doing so. Also, the 60-day period excludes any time taken for an inquiry. In this manner the Bill establishes a normal term for rendering decisions but provides flexibility in the event that the proposal is particularly complex or controversial.
For the person proposing the project there is assurance in the legislation that applications will be handled expeditiously and that the time limit for decisions will be known. This has been the subject of considerable criticism in the past with proponents often facing difficulties in scheduling work in the absence of any indication of anything to the contrary. The new procedures may place pressure on the regulator to make decisions quickly, but this will provide a more equitable system for everyone concerned.
As regards the Railway Safety Act, for any project requiring ministerial approval, and for certain other types designated in the regulations, the completed works may not be placed in operation until an affidavit has been filed with the Minister. This affidavit must testify to the safety of the works and be signed by the professional engineer in charge of the works. This provision requires the proposing party to confirm in writing that works have been carried out in accordance with applicable standards or are otherwise consistent with safe railway operations. The onus to operate safely is placed squarely on the management of the railway companies or any person who undertakes railway work.

There remains a third category of work which may be carried out without reference to the regulator. These would include minor construction or alteration projects which do not have a significant impact on railway safety and which do not have potential to raise objections from other persons on the grounds of safety. The objective in creating these options is to eliminate the processing of routine applications for approval which do not yield benefits in terms of improved safety.
Elowever, Members should note that even in the case of this third category of projects which can be carried out without reference to the regulator, there remain full powers of inspection under the Bill and the power for either the railway safety inspector or the Minister to stop or put restrictions on any operation if a threat to railway safety should rise.
Furthermore, the Minister would have powers to order modification or removal of railway work which is not in accordance with the requirements of the Act.
In providing for the establishment of standards, the Bill states that these may include physical specifications or they may be performance related. This reference to performance standards is intended to encourage a departure from the use of physical specifications, which are usually highly detailed and tend to lock the regulator and the industry into a particular technology. Standards based on performance establish what the railways must achieve in the interest of safety, but do not dictate the method for achieving it.
For example, the existing standards for train brakes are expressed in detailed specifications which are based on the conventional air brake system. In fact, the concern of the safety regulator should only be that a braking system is provided that is capable of stopping moving trains within certain limits. Whether that system be based on air brakes, electric brakes or any other means of stopping a train, depends only on whether the technology does the job safely. The railway safety Bill encourages the regulator to accommodate technological changes which enhance safety without having to change regulations.
Part II of the Bill gives the Governor in Council broad powers to make regulations governing the operation and maintenance of railways. These powers include controls over the safety of railway equipment and the standards to be met by persons employed in positions designated as being critical to the safety of railway operations.
Under these regulations, the Minister will have control over the essential area of operating rules. These rules, which control every facet of the safe operation of railways, include how trains are dispatched and operated by train crews, how equipment is designed and manufactured, and how equipment and track is inspected and maintained.
Members are aware that railway accidents are sometimes ascribed to human error. These almost always involve a violation of the rules which will be covered under Part II of the
Railway Safety Act
Railway Safety Act. By simplifying the procedures and removing these rules from the requirements of the Statutory Instruments Act, this Bill will enable the Minister to implement changes rapidly in the interest of safety and to keep the rules up to date. This was a point of great concern to Mr. Justice Foisy after the collision at Hinton. I am pleased to note on behalf of the Government and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) that Bill C-105 will make it possible for the Minister to respond to Mr. Justice Foisy's recommendation.
The railway safety bill provides flexibility in rule making so that the Minister can tailor rules to special requirements of individual companies. This is particularly desirable in the case of the smaller railways under federal jurisdiction which have no need for many of the rules which have been written with the large main line railways in mind. Nevertheless, the Bill seeks retention of uniformity in rules wherever it is reasonable and practical to do so.
Bill C-105 also allows exemptions from regulations to be granted for specific reasons. This flexible approach will be of particular benefit for carrying out research projects of short duration. The exemption process also could be used to relax certain rules to allow a demonstration of new technology, such as a trial operation of a new rail bus. These exemptions would only be permitted under controlled circumstances which would ensure that there is no threat to safety.

across this country because that is the secret of our success, and it is vital for investment.
There were a couple of points made in the debate which raised questions in my mind but we must realize that transportation is not political. It is an essential service for Canadians. For myself as a Member of Parliament, the transportation system between Charlo, New Brunswick, and the Gaspe is important because there is not a direct line from Ottawa to my office in Carleton. We always hear doom and gloom from the Opposition Parties. But there are no politics, as I said, in transportation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and all members of the Conservative Party will listen to recommendations made by the Opposition with respect to the Railway Safety Act. There is no Conservative, no Liberal, no New Democrat, in fact no one in this country who would want another accident such as the one in Hinton, Alberta. Politics must be put aside. We must hone the Bill. We must respect the recommendations of Mr. Foisy, and we must give the Minister flexibility in the Bill, under special circumstances, so that he can react and react directly. We cannot produce legislation that will cover every possible accident, which is why the Minister will have these powers.
I cannot respond to all the points made in the time I have left. The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) this morning mentioned whistleblowers and unions. He talked about fines, accidents and U.S. deregulation. I believe Hon. Members should know that with deregulation in the United States the accident rate went down, according to the figures 1 have here, for the year 1984. The percentage of accidents has gone down as it concerns railway activities in the United States. In closing I will say I am proud that we have a new Railway Safety Act in Canada for freight and passengers and I am sure that with the co-operation of all Parties, Bill C-105 will be developed into a great Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. friend and colleague on the committee if he would care to express his views as to the adequacy of the Bill in terms of the amount of representation on the consultative committee, which is, one from the union, five from the Government and five from the railroads. Member also tell us his views as to the disproportionate size of the penalties; $10,000 for an individual and $50,000 for a large railroad? Does he consider that a fair proportion?

I thank my hon. colleague for the question. I am sure he realizes that
in terms of railway safety we must ensure that we have equal representation, whatever that might imply. Railway safety, be it on the union side, the railway side or with respect to public input, is very important, and I am sure the Minister has taken that into account in drafting the Bill. At the same time I believe it is very important to note that during the travels of the Standing Committee on Transport to Europe, we found there is more and more an ongoing process there where the employees become part shareholders in the company, which I think would be a very interesting proposition to look at. I do not presume to go beyond what the Minister might say at a later date. Safety cannot be regulated in a sense that we will work 10 per cent of our time on safety and the rest of the time will be spent on other parts of productivity. I believe it is very important that the consultative body be there and be representative of all Canadians who use the service, be it cargo or passenger.
I would like to say at the same time that because of my interest in transport I had the opportunity, as did the Hon. Member for Regina West, to work for several years in the railway business. My father worked for CN for 33 years. So we take this subject very seriously. We want an ideal system for all Canadians so that we can all be happy with our transportation system.

Mr. Speaker, the Act to ensure the safe operation of our railways is one which commands attention and is of an importance that goes well beyond the title of this Bill. What struck me in reading the first few pages of the Bill is the fact that the Bill does not contain a very important aspect that surrounds the operations of a railway, that is, the environment through which it travels. On not one page was I able to find a reference to the environment, any words with respect to our natural resources, nor any words to show that in drafting the Bill the Government was not only sensitive but receptive to environmental issues.
The Bill makes reference in Clause 5 to compliance with the Navigable Waters Protection Act almost as an afterthought or as an add on. For that one can be grateful. However, as we examine the Bill, over some 75 pages, we have to come to the conclusion that the environment has been forgotten. One wonders where the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) was when this Bill was drafted. Was he consulted? Did he ask to be drawn into the discussions to ensure that environmental concerns were included in Bill C-105? For that matter, where were Members of the Progressive Conservative Party from British Columbia when this Bill was drafted?

1 wish to thank the Hon. Member for Winnipeg- Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) for ensuring that there be an audience on this intervention on the environment.
The fact is that in Bill C-105 the environment has been forgotten. One can legitimately ask in the Chamber as to where the Minister of the Environment was when this Bill was drafted, considering the fact that railway transportation does affect the environment in a number of ways. One can also ask where the British Columbia members of the Tory caucus were when this Bill was drafted, considering the experience that they had directly in British Columbia when it came to the twin-tracking of Canadian National in the Fraser River Valley. As a matter of fact, there are two of us in this Chamber now who travelled to British Columbia in 1985, together with a considerable number of Tory Members from B.C., to investigate first-hand that very situation because of the environmental impact imposed by the proposed twin-tracking of CN in a certain section along the Fraser River.
On page 5 of the Bill, where Clauses 7 and 8 are found, which clauses relate to regulations and to the notice in particular of proposed railway works, there is not one reference to the desirability-indeed I should say necessity-of initiating an environmental impact study or an environmental impact assessment in relation to works coming under this particular legislation and related, of course, to railway works. The environment and the experience made thus far in the environment has been forgotten by the drafters of this Bill. The Government has to carry that responsibility for having ignored this very important aspect.
Every year tracks are widened, as are bridges, and railway works are undertaken. It is high time that when works of this type are proposed, before they are initiated and even considered for approval, environment impact be considered as an
Railway Safety Act
essential part in the legislation that covers these types of works. It is therefore not too late, since I think it would be unacceptable to see this Bill go through the House at third reading, to make amendments in committee to Clause 8 in particular to the effect that environmental impact studies and assessments be made mandatory when it comes to railway works that have an impact on the environment.
In reading through the Bill one comes across some other environmental impacts that deserve attention in this day and age since Bills of this type do not receive approval and passage every year. Usually it is every 10 years that a measure such as this is put forward. Therefore I draw Your Honour's attention to Clause 24 of the Bill which is headed "Regulations" as they affect the removal of trees, brush and weeds along railway lines. A subclause here is desirable which would indicate the Government's readiness to consider the use of alternatives to pesticides when it comes to the clearing of weeds, brush, trees and the like along railway lines.
It is a well established fact that jobs can be created by way of manual clearing as an alternative to the removal by pesticides with chemical substances. The reason that manual removal is preferable is due to the fact that conventional pesticides eventually find their way into water and contaminate our water supply. Over the years we have gradually come to the conclusion that the fewer pesticides we use and the more we reduce our dependence on them the better it is for the quality of our waters. I am sure that that conclusion is one that the Minister of the Environment is aware of and one that he should advance in Cabinet when considering amendments to this Bill, as they will inevitably have to be considered in the not too distant future.
If we move to Clause 44(1) of the Bill, which I am sure has been discussed by previous speakers, Hon. Members will see that there is a description of the consultative committee to be established by the Minister. The public affected by rail transportation is not represented in Clause 44(1). In the clause is the provision for a representative of the Minister, of the Canadian National Railway Company, Canadian Pacific Limited, VIA Rail, one to represent the other railway companies to which this Bill will apply, one member to represent the shippers of rail freight and, finally, one member to represent the Canadian Railway Labour Association. However, the public affected by railway transportation, be it VIA Rail, the transportation of goods in general and, in particular, when it comes to the transportation of dangerous goods, is completely missing. One wonders why it is that there is such an oversight. This clause has to be modified in committee. The consultative group to the Minister, as envisaged in Clause 44, must be expanded to ensure the presence of the public affected by, I would say, at least two members to make any sense. We see that in the Bill there is a provision for representatives of various sectors and for specific interests representing what amounts to seven people.
What I would urge you to do, Mr. Speaker, at this stage is to ensure that an amendment to Clause 44 is carried to make

February 4, 1988
Railway Safety Act
this consultative committee representative of the public interest, the very public that is affected by the operation of railways. In too much of this Bill do we find the mind-set of the railway companies which seem to be operating in a vacuum, not aware that whatever they do in the end affects the public. They are there to serve the public. Therefore, if it comes to a consultative committee, 1 submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the public has to be represented.
In looking at Clause 50, and this is the time to do so because we are at second reading debate, again in this clause the citizens or non-governmental organizations that are interested in transportation matters have to be included in this specific clause for the reasons I stated when discussing Clause 44.
Let me briefly comment on a matter that concerns the city I come from, Metropolitan Toronto, where for some time now the citizenry has been increasingly worried about the safety of neighbourhoods should an accident take place as a result of a derailment or an explosion in a train that is moving dangerous goods.
Over the past four or five years since the Mississauga accident of 1979, an organization called M-TRAC has done a remarkable job of sensitizing public opinion and governments to the potential dangers that do exist, in virtually every large metropolitan urban area across the country.
The Government has appointed a special task force on the Toronto area dangerous goods railway matters. Public hearings have taken place and submissions have been made to that task force. In essence, the issues at stake are the following.
It is desirable to start planning and putting aside the funds necessary to relocate rails that go through densely populated areas. This is a costly operation, but it must be done. It is in the interests of large numbers of the population, particularly in downtown Toronto, because the railway line travels through areas where the number of schools is incredibly high. Apart from that fact, over the decades apartment buildings and low-rise residential areas have developed both north and south and east and west of the downtown railway lines. Hence the necessity for beginning to plan the removal of those railway lines to outside the densely populated areas, and specific alternative routes have been recommended to the task force. Therefore, we hope that the very clear and specific recommendations that have been made to the task force will soon reach the Government for its consideration.
There is also the question of the maximum allowable speed. When it comes to the movement of dangerous commodities through densely populated areas, it is important that the speed does not exceed 40 kilometres per hour. This should apply not only to cars that are full, but also to those that are marked empty. Very often with certain commodities cars that are marked empty are not completely or truly empty, and therefore potentially explosive and dangerous.
We have to respect what could be called a vital function of human observers. Here what stands out as an offensive item of neglect is the recent decision of the CTC to abolish the caboose. We are convinced that, for the basic elements of safety, a train that is hauling dangerous goods and is perhaps half a mile long does require a caboose in order to facilitate signalling to the front in case something goes wrong and can be seen at the end of that moving train. The decision made in December, 1987 by the CTC to remove the caboose must be revisited and reversed.
It is important that funds are available to the railway lines to perform the maintenance and the quality repairs that are needed, particularly in relation to hot boxes, the maintenance of rolling stock, the inspection of tracks and switches and, of course, last but not least, the training of employees.
Submissions have been made to the task force in relation to the transportation of dangerous goods. It is just completing its public hearing in Toronto, and it is in a well advanced stage.
I recognize the fact that Bill C-105 may not be intended to cover the transportation of dangerous goods. But at the same time it contains clauses of consultations with the Minister and the composition of committees for the purpose of consultations, which need to be expanded to include the public, particularly those organizations that are interested in dangerous goods. We welcome the idea of a consultative committee to the Minister, but we are saying that that concept has to be expanded to include interested and competent citizens.
Also, in a Bill like Bill C-105 which deals so intimately with the safe operation of railways, the environment must be included and taken into account, particularly in those clauses of the Bill that deal with railway works, alterations, and changes which are a matter of grave concern to neighbourhoods, farmers, native people, and to other activities that directly or indirectly impinge on the environment. For that reason, it is important that the discussion in committee include considerations that are of an environmental nature, and particularly in light of the experience in recent years, considerations that will permit the inclusion of environmental impact studies and environmental assessments.

Mr. Speaker, it is particularly timely, or perhaps even ironic, that we are debating this legislation today. Earlier the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) spoke about the relationship between stress and safety. He referred to an article entitled, "Stress rides the rails" by Professor Tucker who teaches organizational behaviour at the University of Saskatchewan's College of Commerce.
I mention this at the outset because at this point in time there are other things going on within the railway industry which are adding to the stress to which Professor Tucker relates so well in his article. I am referring to the prolonged period of arbitration which has followed the back to work legislation of August 27, 1987.
February 4, 1988

I am also referring to the fact that there is another group of railway unions in limbo at this point to the extent that the railway has now refused to negotiate with them, has taken the position that the second group will receive whatever is awarded to the first group, and is therefore, no longer willing to bargain, relying instead on the willingness of the Government to play the railway's game. The minute the second group, the railway shopcraftsmen, go on strike, if they were to exercise that option, the railway is confident that the Government would proclaim the sections of the Act that would make the strike illegal. They would have to return to work, with binding arbitrations and eventually have imposed on them the settlement which is being imposed on the ARU, or Associated Railway Unions, the group that precipitated the strike in August 1987.
Mir. Benjamin: It is a stacked deck.

Mr. Speaker, it is what the Hon. Member for Regina West has called a stacked deck. Rail workers know that.
As I told Hon. Members of the House on August 27-and it is even worse now-the morale within the railway industry and on the part of rail workers is at an all-time low for very good reason. It is no wonder when we see the time it has taken the current arbitrator, Mr. Larson, plus the effect of rumours about the extension of the arbitrator's period to as late as even September 1988. In the meantime, while things such as job security are being arbitrated by Mr. Larson for the ARU and are not being arbitrated or negotiated at all for the Shopcraft Unions, the railway is proceeding with what it calls "downsizing". Jobs are disappearing all over the place before any arrangements, contract, or agreement can be reached in respect of job security.
On the front page of The Globe and Mail today we see a story about a memo by senior Vice-President of CNR, Doug Fletcher, indicating to his subordinates that they had better get on with the downsizing of each and every aspect of the railway, anything targeted for downsizing, because of the fear that as we get closer and closer to a pre-election political context it would become more and more difficult for the railway to do so.
On the one hand we see accelerated downsizing while at the same time the hands of the rail unions are tied either by extended arbitration or refusal to negotiate on the part of the companies, depending upon which group of unions we are talking about. It is no bloody wonder that these people are angry and frustrated and talk about taking job action.
It is a marked deck.

It is a stacked deck. It is a marked deck. Rail workers have just about had it with the attitude of the Government toward them as working people. All the Bill does is reinforce that impression. What else could such a Bill do
Railway Safety Act
except to reinforce that impression when it talks about setting up a consultative committee of nine to eleven members and only one of them is to be a representative of rail workers themselves? The rest are to be representatives of the Government or of the railways.
One would have thought that the Government would have had the common decency to have at least a five, five, and five arrangement or something like it. It is an insult. It is just like kicking rail workers in the face to say: "Look, guys, we have a good idea. We will have a consultative committee of 11 people. You can have one of them and the rest will be government and railway people. The committee will be giving advice, giving the railways advice, and you will have a big say in the matter". One would have to be an idiot to think that the proposal of the Government in respect of the consultative committee was anything but an insult to railway workers.
The Bill, whatever good may come of it in the sense that it at least establishes the notion of the Railway Safety Act, which is something the NDP and the CCF before it advocated for years, is greatly overridden by the fact that it is stacked against the employee. I have already mentioned the consultative committee. However, let us consider the question of fines. If an individual is found to be in violation of the Act, he or she can be dinged for $10,000. If the CPR is found to be in violation, it can be fined for $50,000. Wow, a $50,000 fine to the CPR! As the Hon. Member for Regina West and others indicated earlier, this is no more than merely a licence fee to be unsafe. Individuals are to take the rap. Employees are to take the rap. The companies not only get light fines, but they have, along with the Government, majority representation on the consultative committee.
Employees have the dubious privilege of being compelled to tell on themselves when it comes to the relationship with their doctors. They have to tell their doctor what is their job, if they are a locomotive engineer or whatever the case may be. Presumably the doctors also have some responsibility pursuant to the legislation. However, rail workers still have no freedom, no protection, no incentive, and no provision whatsoever within the Bill to tell on the railways when they are practising in an unsafe way.
What has been the case for years, and what has actually worsened, will continue. Railway employees will be in a position where, if they are asked to do something unsafe and report it, or if they are compelled to do something unsafe and report it, they will be subject to harassment by management and persecution by management. It goes on believe me. In fact, over time they are liable to lose their job because they are marked and people are out for them. Or, if they go ahead and do the unsafe thing they were asked to do and an accident happens, then they are really in trouble. Then it is the employee who has to take the rap and the company gets away with murder, literally in some cases. This kind of bind that employees are in, where they are damned if they do and damned if they don't, is completely beyond the scope of the

February 4, 1988
Railway Safety Act
Bill. It does not try to address that very difficult situation in which railway employees find themselves whatsoever.
For that reason I predict that many rail workers will simply see the Bill not as the golden opportunity it could have been for the Government to have done something substantial in the area of railway safety but as more evidence of the fact that in some strange and cruel way they have been targeted by the Government as scapegoats in one series of decisions after another, going back to decisions like the one allowed by the Government in respect of the running of cabooseless trains, to the whole deregulation policy of the Government that has created a situation in which railways will be cutting corners and trying to do everything they can to save a few dollars here and there. In the long run it will cost Canadian taxpayers even more in respect of the cost of derailments and of social and other consequences of this short-sightedness.
I would have liked to have had the opportunity to rise today to debate a set of comprehensive safety measures put before Parliament. We do not have either a set of comprehensive measures or the regulations. We do not even have a set of principles that we could debate on rail safety and its relationship to other things like economic criteria, et cetera. We have nothing laid out. It would have been nice, in the Railway Safety Act, to have had a preamble which stated clearly the supremacy of safety over economic consideration. Is it only oversight that we do not have that, or is it further evidence that the railways, along with a lot of other organizations unfortunately, are being instructed basically to adopt this uncritical, excessive, I would say extremist, bottom-line view of how companies ought to operate, that is, in such a way as to make their employees feel that they are disposable commodities which will be eliminated at the first opportunity?
It is pretty hard to work for a company which is constantly sending out messages that it is nice to have one as an employee but if we could figure out a way to get rid of you tomorrow, we would. That is basically the message which CN and CP have been sending to rail workers for four or five years. The story in The Globe and Mail today reinforces that.
It is no wonder that people are as angry as they are and I can tell you that they will be angrier and that we will have more trouble. The Government will have sat idly by doing the bidding of the railways and the bidding of their own ideological fantasies about deregulations, bottom line, and competition while a very good transportation system went down the drain before their very eyes. I was very glad to see the Flon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) raise the matter of the environment. I see that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is here. The fact that there is no reference to the environment in this Bill is evidence of the fact that in spite of all the rhetoric the notion that environmental considerations, pursuant to the Bruntland report, the national task force on the environment and the economy, and all the other fancy documents to which the Government has affixed its name,
should work themselves into all aspects of government policy has not been absorbed by the Government.
If I were the Minister of the Environment I would be somewhat embarrassed to sit there today knowing that there is no reference to the environment in this major piece of railway legislation. That is not something I would like my counterpart in other countries to know about given some of the things I might have said at international fora with regard to how the Canadian Government was moving ahead to incorporate environmental considerations into ail its legislative actions.
They had an option.

The Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) said that they had an option. They could have done it otherwise. They could have done it better but they did not. They left out the considerations which were mentioned by the Hon. Member for Davenport.
I have received complaints in my riding. The railways think they are a law unto themselves. It has been tough enough trying to regulate the railways without having a Government which is committed to the view that they can do whatever they like and that it is somehow good for everyone if the railways do whatever they like. Without regard for public safety or the environment, in clearing rights of ways beside tracks through residential areas the railways spray whatever herbicide they got the best deal on. All hell would break loose if municipal governments tried to do that without hearings to find out who was allergic, et cetera. The railways just do whatever they like.
The Government has basically said that that is okay, that it will not even cover such things in this legislation. The Government says that if anything comes up there will be a consultative committee to deal with it made up of representatives of the railway, the Government, and one member from labour.
This Bill will do very little indeed unless it is accompanied by very strong regulations. I am sorry, but I have absolutely no confidence that that will be the case. I believe that these regulations will be drawn up by the railways for the railways and, according to this legislation, will even basically be enforced by the railways. Rather than an improvement in rail safety, in the sense that this legislation reinforces all the stress and low moral-related problems on the railway, one could even argue, although only time will tell, that this will actually contribute to lack of safety rather than advance the cause of safety. The Government is to be roundly condemned for that.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Crombie (for the Minister of Transport) that Bill C-105, an Act to ensure the safe operation of railways and to amend certain other Acts in consequence thereof be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to have this opportunity to participate in the debate on the Railway Safety Act, Bill C-105. 1 do not think it comes as much of a surprise or shock to Hon. Members that I have an interest in this area which dates back to the time 1 served in municipal Government, the time of the Mississauga train derailment.
On November 10, 1979, a freight train which was bound from London, Ontario, to the Agincourt marshalling yards in Metropolitan Toronto derailed in Mississauga. Of the some 106 cars on that train, some 19 cars were filled with dangerous materials. Three of those 19 cars were tankers that were loaded with propane and at the time of the derailment, they exploded, shooting great balls of fire into the sky. Another car was filled with chlorine and was ripped apart. The chlorine gas seeped out and spread throughout the entire community.
As a result of that derailment which caused the three cars of propane to explode and the one car of chlorine to be ripped open, some 250,000 people had to be evacuated from their homes and businesses for up to five days. In addition, there were substantial economic losses in connection with that derailment. In fact, when the total bill was in and all of the costs added up, losses were estimated at something in excess of $68 million.
February 4, 1988

That derailment occurred in an area of Mississauga which, in 1979, was a relatively undeveloped area. Notwithstanding that, a quarter of a million people had to be evacuated from their homes and almost $70-million worth of damage was done. If the train had stayed on its tracks for another 20 minutes or so, the derailment would have occurred right in the heart of the City of Toronto, obviously an area of much denser development. One can imagine the economic losses that would have resulted if that had happened and the number of people who, if evacuation was possible in an area of that density, would have had to have been evacuated.
If the train had stayed on its tracks for slightly longer than 20 minutes, perhaps for half an hour, the accident would have occurred right in the heart of my own constituency. As I have indicated in the Elouse on a number of occasions, the main lines of both the CPR and the CNR run right through the heart of my constituency.
That accident occurred some eight years ago now. That seems like a long time ago and some of us are starting to forget it and think perhaps it did not happen or, if it did, the whole problem has been dealt with and solved.
Much to the credit of the Government of the day, led by the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), who was then Prime Minister, a royal commission was appointed to investigate that derailment and see what could be done to ensure that nothing like that would happen again. The commission was headed by Mr. Justice Samuel Grange. It investigated the matter thoroughly, made recommendations, all but two, I believe, of which were implemented. One would think that the problem was solved and we would not have any more problems of that sort. The Grange Commission had apparently discovered what went wrong, made its recommendations, and there should not be any more problems.
In spite of that, approximately two rail accidents occur each year in Metropolitan Toronto involving trains carrying dangerous goods. It has become particularly evident to me that this problem has not been solved because, as I brought to the attention of the House last summer, on July 14, just six or eight months ago, another derailment occurred in my own constituency, very near to the densely populated intersection of Don Mills Road and Wynford Drive. At that time 31 cars of a 103-car train derailed. Fortunately, only one car was carrying dangerous goods, car number 87. Also fortunately, although it was carrying a load of vinyl acetate, it did not derail. If it had, the fire chief for the City of North York indicated he would have ordered an evacuation of people within 2,500 feet of the accident site.
I do not know whether you are familiar with that site or its nature and the number of people and businesses located there, but I can tell you it is very substantial. The apartment communities of Wynford Heights have perhaps upwards of
10,000	residents. The apartment community immediately to
Railway Safety Act
the south, Flemingdon Park, has somewhere in the neighbourhood of 20,000 residents. There are numerous businesses in the area, including a number of major oil companies such as Esso, Shell and Texaco. They all have major facilities there. IBM has its major Canadian plant with about 2,000 employees in that area. All of this, to name just a few. We were looking at a very substantial evacuation and very substantial damage if that one car had been part of the derailment.
That made the whole issue quite clear to me. In spite of the fact that we had a royal commission investigate the Mississauga derailment, in spite of the recommendations which had been made and accepted, in spite of all the new procedures instituted, new technology, and efforts to make sure that a Mississauga derailment could not happen again, in 1987 a derailment of a similar nature occurred again.
One factor that was pinpointed at that time was the speed of the train, which was approximately 40 miles per hour. Immediately to the south of that location by just a few kilometres, there is a voluntary speed limit, self-imposed by CPR, of 25 miles per hour. That voluntary speed limit does not apply where this derailment occurred.
At present about 2,000 hazardous commodities used by Canadian industry are transported by rail every day of the week. They include propane, sulphuric acid, butane, and chlorine. I could go on with a long list. Every day of the week about 25 freight trains carrying those hazardous goods pass through my constituency and Metropolitan Toronto. If a derailment occurs today or tomorrow or the next day, what sort of risks would we be running?
It has been estimated that people within one-quarter kilometre of the line would be at the greatest risk. It has been estimated as well that those within one kilometre on either side of the accident site would have to be evacuated because of the problems of escaping gases. In the Mississauga derailment you may be aware that people within 10 kilometres of the track in either direction were evacuated and that damage was experienced within a half a kilometre of the track on either side. We are looking at a very substantial area of potential damage and potential evacuation, especially when you are talking about a heavily built-up area such as in my constituency and in the bulk of Metropolitan Toronto.
What can be done about this situation other than what has been done to date as a result of the Grange Commission? Another Member of this House referred to the fact that in March of 1986 the then Minister of Transport, now the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), created a task force to look into the problems of the transportation of dangerous commodities in the greater Toronto area. I think that is to the credit of this Government and to the particular credit of the Deputy Prime Minister. That task force has been gathering information, done a number of studies, 12 or more, on the problem, and has been holding public hearings. I had an opportunity during the Christmas break of appearing before it to make representations, as did a great many other people.

February 4, 1988
Railway Safety Act
That task force is looking at things like the potential rerouting of dangerous goods, potential relocation of the rail route itself, and other things like imposing a speed limit on trains carrying dangerous goods.
It is not an easy matter to solve that problem because there are a number of different points of view. There are those who believe that a relocation of the railroad tracks would in fact be shifting the burden from one part of the country to another. However, there is evolving a consensus which I believe will go to Metropolitan Toronto City Council for its endorsement tomorrow. That includes the relocation of the tracks to an area north of the city relatively free from development at this time.
There would be the creation of a buffer zone around the track in conjunction with that, similar to the one they have in the City of Regina. That is a 1,000-foot buffer zone. It could be similar to the one in Edmonton which is an even greater buffer zone of approximately 3,000 feet around the main railroad line that carries dangerous goods. That is the kind of long term solution being considered and around which a consensus is developing.
It is being suggested that in the interim period before such a policy can be implemented, a 25-mile per hour speed limit be imposed on all trains carrying dangerous goods through the Greater Metropolitan Toronto area. That is one way we can deal with this kind of problem. But the other obvious solution is through the Bill before us today.
Bill C-105 specifically deals with railway safety. I believe it gives us another opportunity, as the Parliament of Canada, to address the issue of railway safety and ensure that we are doing everything possible to ensure that there are no accidents of the kind that occurred in the Mississauga derailment.
I was pleased to see and learn that in developing the Bill that is before us today there was a consultative process as with Bill C-74, the Environmental Protection Act. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is in the House at the moment. He followed a consultative process with industry, environmental groups and labour in developing the Environmental Protection Act. That is a great credit to the Minister. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) has followed exactly the same procedure in developing this legislation. He also consulted with a wide number and variety of groups.
During his remarks, an Hon. Member mentioned a citizen group in the Metropolitan Toronto area which he commended to the Minister of Transport as a citizens group which should be involved in this process. In fact, it was involved in the process. It is the M-TRAC group which stands for Metro Toronto Residents Action Committee. They formed as a citizens action group after the Mississauga derailment and have been actively involved in promoting rail safety, particularly as it applies to the transportation of hazardous goods, since 1979.
I would like to point out that there are some people in the M-TRAC group who have given of their time and effort on a constant basis to promote rail safety for close to nine years. The group include people like Harold Morrison, Harry Behrend, Rose Dyson, Norm Dyson, Phil Wade and Ying Hope. They are shining examples of citizens who are prepared to give their time and effort on behalf of their fellow citizens, on a voluntary basis, to see that there is safety in our society, our community and our country. They were part of the consultative process and I think we can congratulate them on the effort that they and others have made in helping develop this Bill.
I understand that the Bill implements virtually all the recommendations of the Foisy Commission that looked into the derailment in Hinton, Alberta. I believe that is a major step in the right direction.
Other Members have pointed out their concerns about different parts of the Bill, including the question of the consultative committee and the representation on that committee. I certainly endorse the comments that there should be citizen participation. I would urge the Minister to either amend the Bill or, within the confines of the Bill itself, since he has the right to appoint other people, ensure that there is adequate citizen representation on this consultative committee. I recommend to the Minister that representatives of the M-TRAC organization be included in that.
I know that the Bill is not perfect, and that while it goes a long way there will be criticism. I understand that the Federation of Canadian Municipalities believes there could be improvements, as do the unions. As well, M-TRAC believes there could be improvements.
I am sure that when the Bill goes to committee improvements will be made. I know from past experience that the Minister of Transport has been most willing to see legislation he has put forth improved.
I am convinced that this will be another major step forward in rail safety in this country. I am very pleased with the initiative taken by the Minister of Transport and compliment him for it. I look forward to seeing him strengthen the Bill in committee before it receives third reading.

Mr. Speaker, first 1 want to compliment the Member on what I believe is a very effective and hopefully influential speech on this issue.
I have three questions which arise from my discussions with rail workers and others in the Windsor area who have been very concerned about the question of rail safety there. Many of them have suggested that there will be a great increase in north-south traffic if the trade deal which has been signed goes through. They suggest that this will result in a considerable increase in run-through traffic from the United States, especially if trains, due to lax standards in many states, are not up to safety standards that we hope to have operating in our
February 4, 1988

rail systems here. In fact, various people have given me some examples of the terrible state of some run-through trains.
Does the Hon. Member believe that this Bill needs to be strengthened so that it is clear that control over the safety conditions of run-through trains from the United States into Canada will be very closely regulated, with teeth to back up those regulations?
Second, reports I have had from people in my constituency and my part of Ontario suggest that there have been lay-offs of inspectors. For example, according to reports 1 have received, an extra seven inspectors have been laid off in Sania. Does the Member feel that reducing the number of inspectors is the way to achieve greater safety, or does it not obviously make sense that an increase in inspectors is a crucial part of establishing greater rail safety in this country?
Finally, what is the Member's opinion about the points which have been raised about the role of the whistleblower? For instance, I have a letter that was sent to the chairperson of the negotiating committee in the Windsor area, dealing with points that he raised with respect to rail safety in Windsor during the lead-up to the recent strike. There is a letter from the company which employs him. Among other things the letter states: "1 want to inform you at this time that similar irresponsible conduct will not be tolerated in the future and will prompt a more formal complete investigation".
Is this effort on the part of railway workers to back up safety, to give it publicity, to fight for it publicly, not in fact something that is crucial to assuring safety on the railways and something that should be guaranteed in the Bill itself?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his comments and also for his questions. Dealing with the questions in the order they were asked, he indicated he felt, and that some of his constituents also feel, there will be a substantial increase in north-south traffic as a result of the Canada-U.S. trade agreement. I certainly would hope that would be the case because obviously one of the intentions is to try to open up the American market to Canadian businesses and ensure that we increase the number of jobs in this country. I would see this as a vehicle for doing that. I expect there would be more traffic on the part of Canadian railways going south than there would be on the part of American railways coming north. However, I certainly agree that regardless of what railways these might be, we must insist on safety, and the highest level and degree of safety.
As the Hon. Member knows, there are a number of American railways which operate in our country at the moment. As far as I am aware they have to comply with all of our safety regulations.
Royal Assent
With respect to the number of inspectors, that is a matter that has been raised with me as well from time to time in the Metropolitan Toronto area. Certainly, on the surface 1 would have to agree that it would seem that more inspectors rather than less mean better safety. I would have to be convinced by the railroads in their representations that there was another way of providing for railroad safety other than with more inspectors before 1 would be prepared to agree that we should have a reduction rather than maintaining the ones we have or in fact increasing the ones we have.
With respect to the whistleblower legislation, the Member may be aware, and 1 hope he is aware, that I in fact introduced a motion on whistleblowing into this House in Private Members' Hour. I wish I had been able to have the support of the Hon. Member and his Party, and the support of other Members of the House at that time. Perhaps we would now have whistleblower legislation on a general basis. My particular proposition applied not only to federal Departments and agencies but also applied to all businesses that were federally regulated, which would include the railroads, and it applied to businesses contracting to the Government as well. So I do hope that when I bring forward the proposition again, the Hon. Member will be here to speak in its support.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PARLIAMENT HILL PROPOSED ERECTION OF STATUE OF QUEEN ELIZABETH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the last day that Motion 135 in the name of the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper) was debated, I was indicating my support and the support of others in the House with respect to this measure. I had been saying that after this length of time we should commission the building of a statue of Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II.
I was telling of the visit, as was my friend from Welland, of Her Majesty to the Niagara area in 1973. I remember that it was a rainy day. She buckled her coat around her against the rain and wind. She walked through puddles of water to shake the hands of many a senior citizen, Girl Guide and ordinary citizen of our community, to win the hearts of the thousands that were there gathered. All the while she was doing that, the Duke of Edinburgh was paying his respects to the veterans and the Legions gathered there as well.
Her Majesty has won the respect of many peoples. She has a reputation among senior statespersons as a well informed resource person. Even such distinguished people as Churchill and Charles De Gaulle greatly respected her as a leader and as a person.
General De Gaulle once said that in his time Her Majesty was the most effective statesperson in Europe. The Queen and her family have very frequently been visitors to Canada. Officially, she is the one person who is a non-political person and in a non-partisan way she has travelled from coast to coast. As she travelled from one end of this country to the other, she gained the respect of the people who therein lived; a tradition of democracy in action, a democratic monarchy. She had the support of all democratic peoples wherever they lived and whatever their political or party affiliation might be. Hers was a sympathetic ear, and even in just the telling there was some ease and comfort given to many.
[DOT]	(1710)
Her Majesty the Queen has built up a rapport with the peoples of Canada. It started with a visit by Her father and Her mother in 1939 when daily that telephone call went home to Princess Elizabeth and Princess Margaret telling them of Canada, its changing climate, and how each day the tour took them to a different region or different part, and those stories
were told to those daughters of the then sovereigns of this country.
Then as now, in troubled times royalty gave us strength, encouragement, and unity to face the challenges that confronted us. Later as Queen, she made her first television broadcast in 1957. "Industry and commerce may bring wealth to a country", she told Canadians, "but the character of a nation is formed by other factors. Race, language, religion, culture and tradition all have some contribution to make. I feel proud and happy to be Queen of such a nation".
I wish to join those who think it appropriate to commemorate the thirty-fifth anniversary of the reign of Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II by erecting a statue here on Parliament Hill. To those Members who have reservations about erecting a statue to someone who is still alive, it should be pointed out that the statue of Queen Victoria which now adorns the Hill was proposed and agreed to in 1897 to mark that sovereign's diamond jubilee.
To those Members who feel that such a gesture could be construed as a slight to Canadians of French culture, it should be pointed out that both the man who sculpted the statue of Queen Victoria, the famous Louis-Philippe Hebert, and the Prime Minister of the day, Sir Wilfred Laurier, wanted the monument in an even more conspicuous place than it now is. They wished it to be located on the prestigious site that marked half way between where the Centennial Flame presently is and the entrance to the House of Commons.
Both those French Canadians understood that the British monarchy has nothing to do with ethnicity, race, or language, but everything to do with the constitutional liberty that is ours, and the very words inscribed on the scroll that the Queen extends before her for all to read.
I am pleased and proud to join in support of this motion to commission the erection of a statue to commemorate our great sovereign, the Queen.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PARLIAMENT HILL PROPOSED ERECTION OF STATUE OF QUEEN ELIZABETH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in the debate this afternoon on Motion M-135 brought forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper). I wish to begin by congratulating my colleague for the work that he has done in bringing forward this motion before the House. It is an important one, and it is important to all Canadians. I am pleased to take part in the debate and lend my support to the motion.
I do not have to remind anyone in the House that, when the Fathers of Confederation set about framing our Constitution, they chose to make the new nation a constitutional monarchy. That means we have a Queen of Canada. By an Act of our own Parliament in 1953, and our own deliberate decision in this Chamber, Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II is officially the Queen of Canada.
February 4, 1988

The motion we are discussing today is of special interest to me. I am only the second generation of my family who was born in Canada. My grandfather immigrated to Canada early in the 20th century. 1 learned a great deal from my grandfather about Her Majesty, the Queen. Perhaps it means a little extra to me, although it is important to all Canadians.
Her Majesty is much more than a symbol, she brings a unique perspective to public life. The Queen has a reputation among senior statesmen as one of the best informed and most sensible public servants at that level in the world. As well as being a very charming person Her Majesty inspires affection, along with the respect that she carries throughout the world.
The assets of Her Majesty are non-partisan, she provides knowledge, advice, and encouragement to Ministers of the Crown, as well a being an official patron of the Opposition. Her Majesty's influence in Canada is exercised in two ways, the first being through the activities of the Governor General and the provincial Lieutenant Governors, and secondly Her Majesty's personal visits and participation in special Canadian events.
1 can go back to 1970 when my home Province of Manitoba celebrated its one hundredth anniversary of being part of Canada. Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II visited my home town of Swan River, which is located in west central Manitoba. That was quite an event. For the entire town of approximately 4,500 people it was something that we looked forward to for many months, she arrived in Swan River on the train and spent the better part of an afternoon with us. We are well known in Swan River for having one of the largest rodeos in western Canada, she spent two or three hours viewing some special events put on for her at that time. Virtually everyone from the town and the area came to visit Her Majesty. It was something that the people of the Swan River Valley still talk about.
Again in 1984, shortly after 1 was elected to the House of Commons, I had the special opportunity of greeting Her Majesty when she paid a visit to Canada's National Ukrainian Festival in Dauphin, Manitoba, also in my constituency. That occasion was the second time I was able to meet Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II. Also at that time thousands of people came out and met and saw Her Majesty as she spent two or three hours with us that afternoon. On that particular occasion, she attended Canada's National Ukrainian Festival, and was part of the grandstand audience for approximately one hour that afternoon. It made the event that much more special.
There are thousands of other Canadians from every province and territory in Canada who can tell a similar story, and who can say with full sincerity what the presence of Her Majesty means to events like this. It adds that special majesty and makes the occasion that much more memorable in the minds of Canadians across the country.
Earlier this week 1 read an article in a local newspaper. The article was based on the Super Bowl last weekend, but some of
Statue of Monarch
the comments contained in the article had a lot of truth. The gentleman who wrote the article compared Canadians and Americans. He described Americans as being a confident, energetic people, and how when they are in trouble or when they need something they depend on each other to solve their problems.
In his opinion Canadians are much more cautious, much more conservative, and tend to depend not so much on each other but more on government to solve their problems. Another point he made with which I tend to agree was that we sometimes tend to take ourselves a little too seriously. Sometimes we lose sight of our sense of humour and our sense of pride. In many cases we have become much too critical of ourselves, of our political system, and even of the monarchy at times. I believe these institutions deserve much more respect than we tend to give them as Canadians.
The visits of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth to Canada should inspire and invoke celebration, happiness, and pride in our country, rather than the criticism which quite often happens.
As I mentioned, from personal experience-and I know that other Canadians have had similar experiences-with the visits of Her Majesty, Her very presence adds so much to occasions that are special in themselves. Because of her presence, they are that much better.
By passing Motion M-135, the House could send a clear message to all Canadians that indeed we have great pride in the fact that we are a constitutional monarchy. We could give Canadians no better message than passing a motion which indicates that we will commission the structure of a statue of Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II.
I lend my full and complete support to the motion. I hope that at the appropriate time the Chamber will lend its total support. Once again I congratulate the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton for bringing the matter to our attention.
