speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, indeed I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak in support of Motion M-135 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper). I should like to congratulate him on bringing forward the motion which reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the
advisability of commissioning the structure of a statue of Her Majesty, Queen
Elizabeth II, to be placed on Parliament Hill in commemoration of the thirtyfifth anniversary of Her ascension to the Throne.
As I was thinking about my remarks this evening and what I might say in connection with the motion, my thoughts went back to my recollections of the Queen and the occasions throughout my life in which I have heard about the Queen, seen the Queen, or listened to the Queen.
I am sure that is the same with you, Mr. Speaker, as you have listened to debate on this subject for over three hours

February 4, 1988
Statue of Monarch
now. 1 am sure that you have had thoughts running through your mind about the occasions you have experienced and the recollections you have in connection with the Queen. Mr. Speaker, you are a younger man than I am, so my recollections probably go back a little ways longer than yours do. However, interestingly enough, as I reflected on this subject, the first thing 1 thought about was a record that 1 have in my record library. I have to admit that it is an older record. These days we have tapes and we have 33 1/3 recordings; my kids have some 45s. In any event, this record is a 78. It goes back to the olden days, but it is a recording called "I Can Hear it Now". It was done by a well-known American broadcaster, the late Edward R. Murrow, who turned out three sets of records called "I Can Hear it Now" in which he extracted bits of history and put them into the form of a recording.
The very first of these recordings was of the years which encompassed the Second World War. On that recording he has an excerpt of the two little princesses, as he refers to them, Princess Elizabeth and Princess Margaret. As one listens to the recording, one can picture them standing in the rubble of London with fires and destruction all around them. They were there, little Princess Elizabeth and little Princess Margaret, to broadcast a message to the children of England, to the children of Britain, to the children of the world, from the blitz in London, England during the Second World War. Just as the name of Edward R. Murrow's records were "I Can Hear it Now", I can hear it now in my mind-Princess Elizabeth saying "Good night, Margaret" and Princess Margaret saying "Good night, children", and Princess Elizabeth saying "Good night and good luck to you all". That is really the first thing that I thought about in terms of my recollections of our Queen and the things I was to mention tonight.
Another wartime experience comes to mind in connection with the Queen. It relates to a story that was told me shortly after I came to Ottawa by a really outstanding Canadian by the name of General Shnuk.
General Shnuk was a Polish officer in the Second World War. He commanded the Polish Air Force. He took them out of Poland, escaping from the advancing German and Russian forces. They fought under his command and direction in the Battle of France. Again escaping after the Battle of France, he took them to Britain to fight with the RAF as the Polish Air Force. General Shnuk told me a story of his experiences in England during the Battle of Britain. At that time the RAF was very short of pilots and was looking for replacement pilots. They saw in the Polish Air Force a great potential source of pilots. A great number of negotiations went on between the RAF and General Shnuk on behalf of the Polish Air Force about freeing up Polish pilots to fly for the RAF. Finally, under certain conditions, the Polish Air Force agreed to lend pilots to the RAF. General Shnuk told me that he was picked up one morning and taken to RAF headquarters to sign the agreement whereby Polish fliers would fly in the RAF. About that occasion he said: "Who do you think it was that drove the Jeep which took me over to sign that agreement? It was Queen
Elizabeth". That is another story which comes to my mind when I think of our Queen.
Many other stories come to mind. I remember back in 1947, I guess it was, that the then Princess Elizabeth married Prince Philip. I remember getting up in the middle of the night to listen to the crackling of the radio and the service from Westminster Abbey. That is another memory that I have.
I remember as well the newsreel shots of the time when King George VI died. Queen Elizabeth, then Princess Elizabeth, was visiting in a place in Kenya called "Treetops" with Prince Philip. People went to that resort in Kenya to watch wild animals and it was there that she received the news that her father had died and she had become Queen. I remember those scenes on the newsreels quite vividly. I remember as well her coronation in 1952. By that time our family had a television set and I can remember getting up early again to watch the coronation of the Queen at Westminster Abbey.
I have other much more recent memories of several of the royal tours here in Canada. On one of the last ones her route was to take her past my house. The streets were lined with people for hours in advance and for some reason they changed the route. Everyone was most disappointed, as you will appreciate. However, I have that lasting memory of a time the Queen did not show.
I have many other memories, of course, including the birth of the Queen's children; Charles, Anne, Andrew and Edward. More recent are my memories of her Christmas broadcasts. One of the highlights of Christmas Day for my family is that we listen to the message from the Queen, formerly on radio, now on television.
What sort of messages do these memories of the Queen send to me? I guess the message is that to my mind the Queen personifies everything that is good about human beings. That is the theoretic role that she plays, but in actual fact as a person she seems to do exactly that. She fulfils that role very well. She fulfils the role of a good woman, a good mother, and a good person. If there is anyone who personifies the ideal of family life in this world today I think it is Queen Elizabeth. If she is a role model for all the people of Canada, all the people of the Commonwealth, and all the people of the world, it is the role of how one should live a good life.
In support of this motion I believe that we should have something to symbolize the role model which she has been to us all. I commend this motion to Members of the House.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PARLIAMENT HILL PROPOSED ERECTION OF STATUE OF QUEEN ELIZABETH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words to say in support of this motion today. I think it is certainly a good idea that if we are to have statues of royalty on Parliament Hill we have statues of members of the royalty who mean something in a contemporary context to a lot of Canadians, particularly young Canadians. I say that as someone who has never really known a reigning monarch other
February 4, 1988

than Queen Elizabeth. Elaving been born in 1951 the reigning monarch as far back as 1 can remember has always been Queen Elizabeth.
It is only appropriate that rather than having only statues of Queen Victoria and other people who have long since passed from contemporary Canadian life, a statue to commemorate the thirty-fifth anniversary of Queen Elizabeth II accession to the Throne is something which the Government should consider the advisability of. That is why I rise to speak in favour of this motion.
It was only a few days ago, on January 25, that I rose in this House on Robbie Burns Day to point out the traditional tension which exists between Scotland and England. In speaking to this motion today I have to put aside my inherited Scottish nationalist feelings, as did my grandfather when he came to this country, and say that in spite of that the British constitutional monarchy and the democratic parliamentary system which attends that is something to be valued. One can at least take some solace from the fact that through some of the marriages of the Queen's children, Scottish blood is working its way back into the British monarchy.
My own first memory of the Royal Family, although not of the Queen herself was of the Pan American Games in Winnipeg in 1967. As a member of the Lord Selkirk and District Boy Scout Pipe Band I stood for three hours in the rain waiting for His Royal Highness the Duke of Edinburgh to arrive. We spent some hours after that drying our uniforms.
I had a similar opportunity, also as a member of a pipe band, to wait for hours on end for Princess Anne to arrive at Lower Fort Garry in Manitoba. Finally, I had the opportunity to meet the Queen herself on the occasion of the patriation of the Canadian Constitution being a Member of Parliament at that time and being present for the walkabout in the rotunda of the House of Commons and in the Railway Committee Room.
Given the fact that there are so many Canadians, and that there will come to be more, whose only experience of the British monarchy is Queen Elizabeth II, the motion put forward by the Hon. Member is one which the Government should consider.
While on the subject of statues and women, we ought to be more creative in our use of statues in the parliamentary precincts. We should use them to tell the story of Canadian history. One of the women to whom the Government might also consider the advisability of erecting a statue would be the first woman ever elected to Parliament, Agnes McPhail.
It is certainly the case that the story of women, both in Canada and in the world, is undertold. At the same time as I rise to speak in favour of the motion for the Government to consider erecting a statue of Queen Elizabeth II, I would like to suggest to the House that we consider commissioning other statues to commemorate the roles which other women have played in Canadian political and social life.
Statue of Monarch
I would like to ask the Hon. Member who moved this motion to think about that. It is not that he has deliberately excluded anyone-his motion has to do with Queen Elizabeth II and that is perfectly fair-but there are certainly others whom we could consider and they do not necessarily have to be Prime Ministers or monarchs. Consider, for example, the late J. S. Woodsworth who had a profound impact on Canadian political life but never became Prime Minister. I make a plea not only for the motion but also for recognition of others to the extent that it is possible. We do not want to have the parliamentary precinct cluttered with statues. However, those who are responsible for the commissioning of statues ought to try to think of ways to demonstrate that it is not just in queens, prime ministers and princes that we find human worth and what is to be valued. As Burns himself said, princes and lords are but the breath of kings, an honest man is the noblest work of God.
We should take into consideration in our statue policy that many of the finest achievements of Canadian men and women are achievements that, by their very nature, have put them beyond the pale of those who have come to occupy the positions to which the statues are customarily commissioned. I hope some day that that political reality will be reflected in our policy on the parliamentary precincts.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PARLIAMENT HILL PROPOSED ERECTION OF STATUE OF QUEEN ELIZABETH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed an honour and a privilege for me to take part in this debate this afternoon on the motion of my friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper), a Member whose riding is the neighbouring riding of mine of Ottawa West. I congratulate the Hon. Member for presenting this motion. I believe it is a motion indicative of his fealty to the Crown and of his devotion to Canada. It is indicative also, I would suggest, of his appreciation of Canada and its place in history.
I believe that the preservation of our heritage is as important to Canada's future as good economic policies or social programs. The monarchy is an integral part of that heritage. The symbol of the Crown in Canada is important constitutionally as well as historically. The fact that we are a constitutional monarchy sets Canada apart from the United States, both politically and culturally.
It was loyalty to the Crown that led to the development of much of eastern and central Canada by the Loyalists who fled the 13 colonies following the American Revolution. Two hundred years later, it is the Crown or the Queen in whose name government institutions, from local Crown prosecutors to Parliament itself, function and give force to decisions.
Today's motion deals with a proposal to erect a statue of Her Majesty the Queen here on Parliament Hill. Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II, since coming to the throne in 1952, has served her Canadian subjects well, with grace, energy and devotion. Her Majesty has paid many visits to Canada over the

February 4, 1988
Statue of Monarch
years, helping Canadians celebrate many milestones including Expo '67, the Montreal Olympics and the ceremonies marking the patriation of the Canadian Constitution.
I fondly remember being here on Parliament Hill on Dominion Day in our centennial year of 1967, that great and wonderful year in which Canadian nationalism came to the fore. What a memorable, glorious day that was when Her Majesty joined thousands of other Canadians here on the Hill in proudly celebrating our one hundredth birthday. How appropriate it is, therefore, that her presence be permanently celebrated here on the spot she has visited so often.
Besides paying visits to Canada, Her Majesty has travelled throughout the world. It is interesting to note that in 1957, after a visit to Canada, she paid a state visit to the United States in her capacity not as Queen of the United Kingdom but as Queen of Canada.
When Her Majesty spends time in Canada, she does so as Queen of Canada, not as the head of the Commonwealth. The title, Queen of Canada, is a relatively new one, having been created only in 1953 to reflect Canada's changing role in the world.
In 1957, shortly after she opened Parliament in John Diefenbaker's first Government, Her Majesty addressed Canadians on television and stated in part the following:
Industry and commerce may bring wealth to a country, but the character of a nation is formed by other factors. Race, language, religion, culture and tradition all have some contribution to make, and when I think of the diversity of these factors in Canada today and the achievements that have grown from their union, 1 feel proud and happy to be Queen of such a nation.
Thirty years later, how much more proud Her Majesty must feel, given the Constitutional Accord of 1987 which makes Canada whole once again.
In fact, the Queen's record in regard to French-Canada is undoubtedly equal or better than that of any of her subjects. Long before bilingualism became a political catchword, the Queen was its living exponent. Able to speak French fluently, she has used both languages in speeches throughout Canada. In an address to the Quebec Legislature, she stated:
It is agreeable to me-to think that there exists in our Commonwealth a country where I can express myself officially in French-one of the more important languages in our occidental civilization.
The character the Queen bestows upon the state goes so far as to legitimize and even honour that part of the community which opposes the Government, Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. It is a reality then when Parliament is dissolved in the Queen's name and the Royal Proclamation reads:
Whereas we are desirous and resolved, as soon as may be, to meet our people of Canada, and to have their advice in Parliament: we do make known our Royal will and pleasure to call a Parliament, and do further declare that by the advice of our Privy Council for Canada, we have this day given orders for issuing writs, for calling a Parliament in Canada.
There are those who suggest that the monarchy has no role in our modern society. This attitude, with respect, betrays a lack of understanding and appreciation both of history and of
our Constitution. In my experience, it does not reflect the thinking of the young Canadians with whom I have come in contact since my election and with whom I have discussed the role of the monarchy.
I think of my own 11-year-old daughter Jennifer and her friends who have a keen, abiding interest in the royals, not just Di and Sarah, although I must say that they are special favourites, but the entire Royal Family. They recognize, as I think most thoughtful Canadians do, that the Queen and what she symbolizes contributes to our uniqueness and special character in the northern half of this continent and indeed in the world.
Her Majesty, Elizabeth II has always acted as a constitutional monarch, co-operating with and assisting her Ministers as well as accepting their advice. Some 36 years of direct involvement in Canadian affairs as sovereign in addition to her apprenticeship to that role have made her counsel highly valuable. I know how important that counsel has been to our own Prime Ministers over the years as it is on a weekly basis to Prime Ministers in London. As the Queen told Canada in 1977:
My family's association with this country over many generations allows me
to see and appreciate Canada from another viewpoint, that of history.
That historical perspective, perhaps helped by being viewed from across the Atlantic, is, 1 would suggest, a perspective that many of us could benefit from in our analysis of the issues that come before this Chamber and the Parliament of Canada.
Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II has made so many contributions to Canada that I think it is only fitting that Canadians honour her through the erection of a statue here on Parliament Hill, the seat of Her Majesty's Government in Canada. Once again, I congratulate the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton for bringing this suggestion to the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Nepean- Carleton (Mr. Tupper). We are all very busy, either in our ridings or in this House helping to formulate and guide legislation through. There are many occasions when something like this passes by unnoticed, but our hon. friend and colleague did not let it pass by. He took the time to put this legislation before us and I commend him for that.
Canada is a proud country. It is proud of its history. The Royal Family has always played a very important part in Canadian history. For us, no royal figure has played a more prominent role than Queen Elizabeth II. She is truly the Queen of Canada.
When considering statues around Parliament Hill, I sometimes think we do things backwards. I do not know why we have waited so long. We have commissioned statues for Parliament Hill and we have discussed doing it for great people. Do not misunderstand, they are all deserving, but I
February 4, 1988

think a statue Her Majesty should have been considered before this. Therefore, let the Thirty-third Parliament be remembered as the Parliament which cared enough to honour our very own Queen.
I have enjoyed the debate very much. Hon. Members have reminisced so much that 1 have learned a great deal about their lives. 1 also have a sampling of the Queen's very busy life in Canada. Many Canadians on occasion regard the Queen as being way over there in Great Britain and not really attached to Canada. That is wrong. 1 shall not go into this at great length but the Queen succeeded to the throne on February 6, 1952. Skipping down to 1956, the Queen assigned coats of arms to the Yukon and Northwest Territories. In 1957 she became the first reigning monarch to open a Canadian Parliament. If I may quote briefly, she said:
I greet you as your Queen. Together we constitute the Parliament of
Canada.
In 1960 Prince Andrew was born to the Queen, on February 19. Her Majesty honoured the three-quarter million member Canadian Legion that year as well by giving it the prefix Royal. In 1965 the Queen proclaimed the Maple Leaf flag, on January 28. She approved the design of the flag of the Province of Ontario on April 12. In 1967 she approved the Canadian Armed Forces ensign. She presided at the Centennial of Confederation weekend and addressed both Houses of Parliament. In 1969, on Dominion Day, she invested Prince Charles as Prince of Wales at Carnarvon Castle. In 1973 she toured Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Saskatchewan and Alberta. She spent Dominion Day in Charlottetown for the province's centenary. In Toronto she made a widely-acclaimed speech, and I quote:
I want the Crown to be seen as a symbol of national sovereignty belonging to
all. It is not only a link between Commonwealth nations, but between
Canadian citizens of every national origin and ancestry.
In 1977 the Queen celebrated her Silver Jubilee in Ottawa, in October, and opened the third Session of the Thirtieth Parliament. She said at that time:
I dedicate myself anew to the people and the nation I am proud to serve.
Going down to 1981, the Queen held an investiture of the Order of Military Merit of Canada at Buckingham Palace. She declared to her Canadian Privy Council her consent to the marriage of the Prince of Wales. In March she approved a new flag for the Governor General. In 1982, as some of my colleagues have referred to, the Queen proclaimed the revised Canadian Constitution at Ottawa on April 17.
Those are just some examples of the extent to which the Queen visits and cares about Canada.
I just want to say that the Bill put forward by my hon. colleague has my unequivocal support. We very badly need a statue of the Queen of Canada for all Canadians to view on the grounds of this Parliament. It will remind everyone in Canada that Her Majesty is our Queen.

FARM CREDIT CORPORATION-LACK OF FINANCIAL RESOURCES/FARM FORECLOSURES
['The motion to adjourn the House is now deemed to have been adopted. Accordingly this House stands adjourned until tomorrow morning at 10 a.m., pursuant to Standing Order 3(1).']

Mr. Speaker, last September I put a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and pointed out that the Farm Credit Corporation had slipped into a position of negative equity of $124 million, making it essentially insolvent. That was the state of insolvency of the Farm Credit Corporation on April 1 last year. I am told that by April 1 this year the level of insolvency will be over $300 million. The Farm Credit Corporation is in a terrible situation.
Many Canadians may not be too worried about the level of insolvency of a Crown corporation of the federal Government, but this corporation is charged with the responsibility of providing long term credit at stable levels in order to help some
50,000	farmers in this country who are either insolvent or facing serious financial difficulty. 1 asked the Prime Minister how this corporation could carry out this responsibility when it, itself, is insolvent?
The greatest failure of the Government in terms of agriculture has been the handling of the farm debt crisis. That crisis was well catalogued in the fall of 1984 by a report of the Farm Credit Corporation which indicated that thousands of farmers were in serious financial difficulty.
The Minister did little during that three and one-half year period. It took him almost a year and a half to bring in legislation for a Farm Debt Review Board. The legislation had no teeth but simply established a mechanism for consultation between farmers and their creditors. If the banks decided not to do anything, they simply waited out the stay of execution for the 120 days as prescribed, then went ahead with the foreclosure. It took years to get even that mechanism in place.
Next, the Minister introduced stay of foreclosures on people who had mortgages with the Farm Credit Corporation. He maintained that policy for some 18 months, without providing money to the Farm Credit Corporation or giving any meaningful programs to reschedule that debt.
The debt of Canadian agriculture during the last three and one-half years has grown from some $19 billion to approximately $22 billion, at a time when farm incomes are being chopped and the entire system is deteriorating.
When the Outlook conference was held and the Government announced all of its massive initiatives to help Canadian agriculture, it is interesting to note that it included the announcement that it would have to write off some $500 million more during the next three years. It is another indication of a tremendous opportunity lost, where the Government simply held on to land during the last three and a half years, rather than take a pro-active approach to find ways to reschedule debt and save literally thousands of farmers.
There are more farmers in serious difficulty now than in the fall of 1984 when the Government took office. Moreover, for over a year the chairman and vice-chairman of the Farm Credit Corporation were putting forward recovery programs.
All of those were rejected by the Government. Finally, in December, it discharged the chairman and vice-chairman and brought in new people, one from the Treasury Board and another who was not an active farmer, to take charge of the Farm Credit Corporation and try to come up with a recovery program. Since then a new survey has been announced to find out how serious the financial difficulty is.
What we need is not more surveys. What we need is a proactive recovery program to try to keep as many as possible of the 50,000 farmers who are insolvent or in serious financial difficulty on the farm. I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will announce tonight a complete revamping and recovery package for the Farm Credit Corporation so that farmers who are facing the loss of their land will know the Government is finally coming to its senses and putting in place a program not only to put this Crown corporation on a sound financial footing but to help the thousands of farmers who need help today.

-we are going to have to take steps to pul the FCC on a firmer footing. I

subtopic: HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-DIOXIN IN PAPER PRODUCTS- CHLORINE BLEACHING PROCESS
HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-DIOXIN IN PAPER PRODUCTS- CHLORINE BLEACHING PROCESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you look like a coffee drinker to me. I will bet that, like myself, you really do not feel human in the morning until you have had your first cup of coffee. I can see by the way you are nodding your head that that is true. 1 do not think you should feel badly about this, Mr. Speaker, because there are thousands, probably millions of people like you and I who need that cup of coffee in the morning before we feel human. Flow do you go about making your coffee, Mr. Speaker? I use a Melitta coffee maker. When 1 get up in the morning I fill the container of the coffee maker with water and then 1 get out the coffee. Coffee is an awful price now, is it not, Mr. Speaker?
1 get out the coffee and I put it in the filter. I put that into the coffee maker and turn on the switch. Before very long I have a wonderful cup of coffee. I know you would enjoy having a cup of coffee with me, Mr. Speaker.
Lately, I really have not felt the same way about my coffee as I did before. I do not really look forward to it now the way I used to. The reason for that, and 1 bet you probably feel the same as I do, Mr. Speaker, is because I have read in newspaper reports that traces of dioxin have been found in the paper filters for coffee makers.
Dioxin is a deadly, deadly toxic chemical. Fortunately, the most deadly kind of dioxin has not been found in the paper filters for coffee makers. But the most deadly kind of dioxin there is is very deadly indeed. Just a trace of dioxin of that sort can cause birth defects. It can cause cancer and damage to the immune system. A level of safe exposure to that kind of dioxin has never been established.
Fortunately for you and I, Mr. Speaker, as coffee drinkers, traces of that sort of dioxin have not been found in those coffee filters as yet. However, it is no wonder when we read the stories that you and I, Mr. Speaker, will look very carefully now at those coffee filters that we use in the mornings. It is no wonder that Your Honour and 1 watch the coffee dripping through those filters with much more intense interest than we ever did in the past. It is no wonder that Your Honour and I think twice as we sip our coffee that has come through those paper filters each morning.
It is not just the paper coffee filters in which dioxin has been found. It has been found in other forms of paper products as
Adjournment Debate
well. I refer to facial tissues, and I am seriously thinking of going back to the linen handkerchief. It has been found in paper plates. Just think of all the paper plates used by McDonald's and Burger King. It has been found in paper towels. In those types of paper products traces of the most deadly kind of dioxin known to mankind has been found.
When you and I think about this, Mr. Speaker, it is only logical that we feel that in using these products there is a transfer of the dioxin from the product to ourselves. What is causing this sort of thing? We do not really know for sure. However, the paper companies and the pulp and paper industry feel and suspect that this dioxin is formed in the bleaching process for paper. Chlorine is used in this bleaching process. Our pulp and paper industry uses this chlorine. The pulp and paper industry in the United States uses chlorine in the bleaching process as well.
You may remember, Mr. Speaker, that just last week the Department of the Environment conducted some tests on pulp and paper mills and found in and around a pulp and paper mill in Nanaimo, British Columbia, traces of dioxin.
In Europe, chlorine is not used in the paper bleaching process. An oxygen bleaching process is used instead of chlorine. It is used because it has been claimed that the oxygen process does not produce dioxin and that the process for paper is more safe. I wonder why it is that we are not using that oxygen process here. If it is safer and does not produce dioxin, and if we used it here, you and I, Mr. Speaker, would feel a lot better when we had that cup of filtered coffee every morning.
1 ask you, Mr. Speaker, how about it? I put the same question to the Parliamentary Secretary, how about it, Mrs. Parliamentary Secretary? When are we going to get the pulp and paper industry in Canada to start using an oxygen bleaching process instead of a chlorine bleaching process for paper that causes and results in dioxin in paper products?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Shirley Martin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-DIOXIN IN PAPER PRODUCTS- CHLORINE BLEACHING PROCESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with you and my hon. colleague in looking forward to that cup of coffee in the morning to make myself human.
The Hon. Member asks that the federal Government require Canadian pulp and paper mills to switch from the chlorine bleaching process, now used in Canada, to oxygen bleaching, as used in many Swedish mills. The reason for this is the detection of low levels of the dioxins 2, 3, 7, 8 TCDD in paper products, and also in effluents from some U.S. mills that use chlorine bleaching.
I believe it is premature to conclude that such a conversion is immediately required. Both the Department of the Environment, which regulates environmental matters, and Consumer and Corporate Affairs, which regulates product exposure, have been advised by National Health and Welfare that, based on a preliminary risk assessment, it is unlikely that there are any

February 4, 1988
Adjournment Debate
significant health risks associated with dioxins in paper products. National Flealth and Welfare will conduct a quantitative assessment when studies on the migration of dioxins from paper products are complete. That Department is also monitoring work which is under way in this area in the United States.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has formed an interdepartmental task force to address product concern issues, and is interacting with officials of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency in this area. The Departments of National Health and Welfare, Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and Environment are represented on this task force.
In addition, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has formed a task force with Environment Canada to determine the amount of dioxin released from the Canadian pulp and paper industry, the levels in the environment, and to recommend ways and means of controlling releases.
It has been advocated by some, as well as my hon. colleague across the floor, that the oxygen bleaching process as a means of avoiding dioxin formation should be used, rather than the present chlorine bleaching process. Oxygen prebleaching is now fairly extensively used in Sweden. In fact, eight of the fourteen Swedish bleached kraft mills now use it. However, the Swedes use oxygen prebleaching to limit total organic chlorine discharges and not specifically dioxin discharges. The process is being implemented under a Swedish action plan that has the goal of reducing total organic chlorine compound discharges to 1.5 to 2 kilograms per tonne of product by 1991. At present, one Canadian mill uses oxygen prebleaching. That is the E. B. Eddy Mill at Espanola, Ontario.
We are seeking reliable information on the specific levels of dioxins formed and released with oxygen bleaching. It is possible that dioxin formation may still occur with the oxygen prebleaching process, as chlorine and chlorine compounds still continue to be used. However, the amount of chlorine used is less than that required for conventional chlorine bleaching.
The departmental task force within Environment Canada is charged with assessing the effectiveness of this and other technologies that may be used to reduce dioxin formation. Environment Canada officials have held preliminary discussions with the Swedish Environmental Protection Board, and will have further consultations with them and environmental authorities of other countries concerned with this issue.
Thorough assessments needs to be performed to determine dioxin levels in effluents and products, the risks posed, and the effectiveness of various technologies to reduce their presence. This work is now under way. Environment Canada will be reporting on progress.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 22, 1988, I put a question to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), in view of the fact that the Ontario Ministry of Health published information with regard to the high cost of prescription drugs and the fact that it had conducted a survey of some 1,000 drugs and found that the prices of most of those drugs were rising beyond the Consumer Price Index. In some instances they were rising in excess of 100 per cent and, in a particular instance, in excess of 250 per cent.
As usual with that particular Minister, his answer to my question was totally unsatisfactory. In fact, I quoted for the Minister's consumption his own words as reported at page 10666 of Hansard wherein he said:
One of the consequences of the activity of the Senate is to raise once again
the spectre of whether drug prices will increase at a faster rate than the cost of
living. They will not. I maintain that those who claim that they will are wrong
and have no basis for making that claim.
Those were the Minister's comments away back then.
From time to time I have been required to purchase medication for my two daughters, Leigh-Ann and Jennifer. I have found in tracing the prices of drugs for young girls five and six years old that the prices have increased. It is not a phenomenon which has occurred only in the Province of Ontario. It has occurred in other jurisdictions as well.
What is perhaps very appalling is that the Government of Canada, in particular the Minister responsible, has not seen fit to act on behalf of Canadian consumers. He has failed to exercise the responsibilities given to him as Minister. Also, he seems to want to slough off the issue as something for which they were not responsible.
If one were to check Hansard and the proceedings of the various standing committees, in particular the legislative committee seized with Bill C-22, one would find clear and unequivocal statements by myself, and indeed by other Hon. Members, that in effect the mere tabling of the legislation, by providing to multinational corporations an extended monopoly of upwards to 10 years, would result in higher drug prices for Canadians both by brand name and perhaps by generic.
The reason we said so at that time was that the multinational corporations would choke off the viability of generic firms, thereby necessitating them either to float money on the markets and/or to increase the price of their particular product to generate additional revenues.
A few months, have gone by since the passage of Bill C-22, and what we predicted has come true-higher drug prices for Canadians.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has abdicated his responsibility. He refuses to give a directive to the new Drug Prices Review Board in which I must admit I do not have much faith. He refuses to exercise the persuasive
February 4, 1988

powers that are tied into that particular board. He refuses to give it a directive to investigate, when it is up and going, the drugs which have been reviewed by the Ontario Ministry of Health.
There has been an abdication of the responsibilities to consumers, to young people such as my daughters Jennifer and Leigh-Anne who, through their parents, have to pay higher costs for their medication, to senior citizens, to poor people, and to people on fixed incomes across the country. This was a time for the Government of Canada to seize the opportunity and act forcibly on behalf of Canadian consumers.
I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will stand in her place and share with us a new attitude, a new behaviour by the Government toward Canadian consumers. I hope that we will not get the same pat answers which we have been getting from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs for well over a year with regard to the high cost of prescription drugs.
It is time for new action. It is time for a new attitude by the Government which is quickly losing the confidence and respect of Canadians on a host of consumer-related issues.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Shirley Martin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-DIOXIN IN PAPER PRODUCTS- CHLORINE BLEACHING PROCESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government does not have to change its attitude toward consumers because it is and always has been concerned about consumers and will continue to be in the future.
It has been stated on numerous occasions that Bill C-22 has been carefully designed to balance a variety of objectives in respect of the pharmaceutical industry in Canada. Among these are increased research and development, increased chemical manufacturing, a healthy and growing generic drug industry, improved health care and, very important, the expansion of consumer protection in respect of drug prices.
Bill C-22 is both an instrument of industrial policy and, at the same time, an instrument designed to ensure that Canadian consumers have access to fairly priced drugs.
Members of the Opposition have consistently maintained that Bill C-22 fails to provide this guarantee. In fact, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) has said that drug prices in the Province of Ontario are rising faster than the Consumer Price Index because of Bill C-22. I
Adjournment Debate
point out that drug prices across Canada have risen more than the Consumer Price Index in each of the last 10 years. Bill C-22 did not exist then. How does the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond answer this?
In fact, members of the Opposition have failed to see, as they usually do, that Bill C-22 for the first time provides a new mechanism which will ensure fairer prices for consumers. The instrument the Bill created to ensure that prices will not get out of hand is the Patented Medicine Price Review Board.
In fact, the Board began start-up procedures over a month ago when the Chairman, Dr. Harry Eastman, and ViceChairman, Dr. Robert Goyer were appointed. At this time, through the development of effective regulations, the Board is gearing up to address not only the question of increases in Ontario which were the subject of considerable press attention as noted by our hon. friend, but also to address the prices charged for all patented drugs.
This is an important distinction because Bill C-22 provides the consumer much wider protection than was available under the previous compulsory licensing system. It is interesting to note that without Bill C-22 the price increases reported by the Province of Ontario would not have been an issue as there would have been no board with the potential to address the issue. Canadian consumers would have absorbed these increases because without Bill C-22 consumers have no way of knowing whether they are paying fair prices for their patent medicines.
The Board collects the necessary data to rule on the appropriateness of the drug prices and it will analyse, not only the information provided by companies themselves but also information from individuals and the provinces.
I am confident that with all the protective measures in place the interests of Canadian consumers are in good hands. The Minister has not abdicated his responsibility on Bill C-22 because the Board does exist and will examine this and other issues for the benefit of all Canadians in a way which was not previously possible.
